title: Opinion of the European Economic and Social Committee – My Voice, My Choice: for safe and accessible abortion (own-initiative opinion)
text:
Official Journal of the European Union
EN
C series
C/2026/1957
28.4.2026
Opinion of the European Economic and Social Committee
My Voice, My Choice: for safe and accessible abortion
(own-initiative opinion)
(C/2026/1957)
Rapporteur :
José Antonio MORENO DÍAZ
Advisor
Lidia FERNÁNDEZ MONTES (to the rapporteur, Group II)
Rugilė BUTKEVIČIŪTĖ (to Group III)
Plenary Assembly decision
18.9.2025
Legal basis
Rule 52(2) of the Rules of Procedure
Section responsible
Employment, Social Affairs and Citizenship
Adopted in section
26.11.2025
Adopted at plenary session
21.1.2026
Plenary session No
602
Outcome of vote
(for/against/abstentions)
196/12/11
1.    Conclusions and recommendations
1.1.
The European Economic and Social Committee (EESC) highlights and welcomes the work on the European Citizens’ Initiative propelled by the My Voice, My Choice movement, in finding a pragmatic way to address securing access to women’s right to abortion in the EU.
1.2.
In response to this initiative, the EESC reiterates that abortion is and must be a human right that is inseparable from many other rights, not just the right to health, and that the genuine and effective exercise of this right must be ensured through an intersectional approach.
1.3.
The EESC calls on the European Commission to submit a proposal for financial support for Member States that would allow anyone in Europe who still lacks access to safe and legal abortion to safely terminate a pregnancy, in accordance with national law.
1.4.
The EESC reaffirms that the denial or obstruction of abortion care constitutes institutional gender-based violence within the meaning of the Istanbul Convention and Directive (EU) 2024/1385 of the European Parliament and of the Council  ( 1 ) . Member States must therefore include access to abortion in their systems for preventing gender-based violence and supporting victims, and specifically in their public health systems.
1.5.
The EESC stresses that, in accordance with Article 2 of the Treaty on European Union (TEU), Article 8 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU) and Articles 1, 3, 21 and 35 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights, access to safe and legal abortion is part of the Union’s duty to uphold the dignity, integrity, and equality of women.
1.6.
The decision to terminate a pregnancy must lie solely with the woman concerned, who must decide independently and free from coercion, disinformation and stigma.
1.7.
The EESC stresses that access to safe, legal abortion must be accompanied by policies and programmes that ensure informed freedom of choice and comprehensive sexuality education for all people. Every woman and girl has the right to make autonomous and evidence-based decisions about their body and reproductive life without being subject to coercion, disinformation or stigma.
1.8.
Comprehensive sexuality education – as stipulated in Article 14 of the Istanbul Convention, in the EU Strategy on the Rights of the Child and in UNESCO’s International technical guidance on comprehensive sexuality education – is essential to prevent unwanted pregnancies, promote gender equality and protect against sexual violence.
1.9.
The EESC calls on the Member States to integrate comprehensive, scientifically rigorous and age- and ability-appropriate sex education into school curricula and relevant EU programmes, to introduce monitoring and evaluation of these programmes and to ensure that healthcare professionals are trained to respect informed consent and patient autonomy.
1.10.
The EESC believes that the European Commission will need to clarify the arrangements for EU funds to finance the exercise of this right, and for the financial support mechanisms for civil society organisations that provide funds to women who are considering abortion.
1.11.
In the absence of data to support the proper implementation of effective policies, the EESC recommends that the European Institute for Gender Equality (EIGE) and Eurostat collect disaggregated data on sexual and reproductive health and rights.
1.12.
The EESC considers it necessary to strengthen these women’s rights in the face of attacks from the far right and fundamentalist groups.
2.    General comments
2.1.
The My Voice, My Choice campaign offers EU citizens the chance to make women’s lives freer, safer and better – wherever they live in our Union, whatever conditions they may find themselves in.
2.2.
In this regard, the campaign highlights that the lack of access to abortion in many parts of Europe not only puts women at risk of physical harm but also puts undue economic and mental stress on women and families, particularly those living in conditions of social, economic, job or cultural insecurity that can afford it the least.
2.3.
The EESC therefore calls on the European Commission to submit a proposal for financial support for Member States that would allow anyone in Europe who still lacks access to safe and legal abortion to safely terminate a pregnancy, in accordance with national law.
2.4.
This solution could take the form of an opt-in mechanism open to Member States on a voluntary basis. Those who opt in would then receive financial support from the EU to compensate for the weight of this solidarity effort. The European citizens’ initiative with the same title falls within the framework of the EU’s remit for providing support.
2.5.
The initiative has received 1 124 513 signatures in support from people from Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, Croatia, Cyprus, Czechia, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Hungary, Ireland, Italy, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malta, Netherlands, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Slovakia, Slovenia, Spain and Sweden. The EESC highlights the effort involved in collecting these signatures.
2.6.
The initiative, registered on 10 April 2024, was validated on 1 September 2025, which clearly indicates that it falls within the remit of the EU and outside the remits of the Member States.
2.7.
The EESC fully supports this initiative, which is a further step towards achieving safe, legal and accessible abortion for women in the EU.
3.    Specific comments
3.1.
Access to safe and legal abortion must be a human right. It is matter of human rights, and ensuring this access is the best way to protect women’s bodily autonomy and reduce maternal mortality.
3.2.
The decision to terminate a pregnancy must lie solely with the woman concerned, who must decide independently and free from coercion, disinformation and stigma.
3.3.
Member States have an obligation to respect, protect and implement human rights, including those relating to health and the right to bodily, sexual and reproductive autonomy. When safe, legal abortion services are unjustifiably restricted or not fully available, it restricts not only access to abortion but also the right to abortion itself, which could jeopardise a variety of other internationally protected human rights. These include the right to non-discrimination and equality; the right to life, health and information; the right not to be subjected to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment; the right to privacy and physical integrity and autonomy; the right to decide how many children to have and how far apart; the right to freedom; the right to share in the benefits of scientific advancement; and the right to freedom of conscience and religion.
3.4.
These rights are laid down in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and protected through numerous international agreements, such as the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (ICESCR), the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR), the Convention against Torture (CAT), the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (CEDAW), the Council of Europe Convention on preventing and combating violence against women and domestic violence (Istanbul Convention) and the Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC), as well as in regional agreements in Africa, America and Europe.
3.5.
Article 12(1) of the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women states that ‘States Parties shall take all appropriate measures to eliminate discrimination against women in the field of health care in order to ensure, on a basis of equality of men and women, access to health care services, including those related to family planning.’ More specifically, CEDAW General recommendation No 35 explicitly states that the criminalisation of abortion constitutes a violation of women’s sexual and reproductive health and rights and a form of gender-based violence, and urges states to repeal any legislation criminalising abortion.
3.6.
Under Article 2 TEU, Article 8 TFEU and Articles 1, 3, 21, and 35 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights, access to safe, legal abortion is part of the Union’s duty to uphold the dignity, integrity, and equality of women.
3.7.
The Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities commits States Parties to ‘provide persons with disabilities with the same range, quality and standard of free or affordable health care and programmes as provided to other persons, including in the area of sexual and reproductive health and population-based public health programmes’.
3.8.
Furthermore, the UN Human Rights Committee has specifically recognised that a woman’s decision to voluntarily terminate her pregnancy is part of the right to privacy and that not respecting a woman’s decision to undergo a legal abortion constitutes a violation of the right to privacy, including in cases where the judiciary interferes with such a decision  ( 2 ) .
3.9.
More recently, sexual and reproductive health and rights have been included in the UN Sustainable Development Goals’ targets, specifically Target 3.7 (ensure universal access to sexual and reproductive health-care services, including for family planning, information and education, and the integration of reproductive health into national strategies and programmes) and Target 5.6 (ensure universal access to sexual and reproductive health and reproductive rights as agreed in accordance with the Programme of Action of the International Conference on Population and Development and the Beijing Platform for Action and the outcome documents of their review conferences).
3.10.
Equally, the EESC opinion on Violence against women as a human rights issue: state of play of measures across the EU  ( 3 ) notes with concern that the restrictions on the free and safe voluntary termination of pregnancy and the harassment suffered by women (particularly in the vicinity of clinics) have not been considered specific forms of violence against women, and recommends legislation on safe zones around clinics to prevent harassment and intimidation.
3.11.
The guarantee of women’s sexual and reproductive rights should include the right to be free to decide on the voluntary termination of pregnancy and the right to abortion, as well as effective access to abortion. In the face of systematic attacks by fundamentalist and extreme right-wing groups, the EESC considers it necessary to adopt legal measures in the Member States to guarantee not only this right but also its free exercise.
3.12.
The EESC notes that, even where abortion is legal, regional and social disparities continue to limit effective access. In several rural, poorer, or culturally conservative areas, inadequate medical infrastructure is compounded by stigma, moral pressure and entrenched patriarchal norms, in some local contexts still influenced by traditional patriarchal honour codes or strong community pressures. These conditions foster fear, silence and even secret births, with serious consequences for physical and mental health. The EESC stresses that ensuring effective access requires not only legal and institutional guarantees, but also educational and social measures to combat stigma and protect women’s autonomy.
3.13.
The EESC reaffirms that the denial or obstruction of abortion care constitutes institutional gender-based violence within the meaning of the Istanbul Convention and Directive (EU) 2024/1385. Member States must therefore include access to abortion in their systems for preventing gender-based violence and supporting victims, and specifically in their public health systems.
3.14.
On 4 March 2024, France enshrined guaranteed freedom to abortion in its Constitution, making it the first country in the world to make abortion a constitutional right, with the aim of establishing a safeguard against the backsliding on the right to abortion in the EU and worldwide. As early as January 2022, Emmanuel Macron, holder of the rotating Presidency of the Council of the European Union at the time, proposed to the European Parliament that the right to abortion be included in the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights.
3.15.
Research shows that an intricate network of 275 players, which received funding amounting to USD 1,18 billion between 2019 and 2023, is devoted to undermining sexual and reproductive rights in Europe  ( 4 ) . The EESC stresses the need for a coordinated, proactive European response to protect these rights.
3.16.
In view of the above, the EESC, like other international bodies, considers that access to sexual and reproductive health and rights – including guaranteed effective access to safe, legal abortion services – is a fundamental right; that sexual and reproductive health and rights are essential for upholding human dignity and are linked to combating sexual and gender-based violence and achieving gender equality and other human rights, such as a person’s right to life, health, privacy, security of the person, non-discrimination, equality before the law and freedom from torture and other cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.
3.17.
The EESC points to the EU’s commitment to ensuring that all women and girls are guaranteed full bodily autonomy and full and autonomous control over and the right to decide freely on matters related to their sexuality and sexual and reproductive rights, free from discrimination, coercion and violence  ( 5 ) .
3.18.
Comprehensive sexuality education – as stipulated in Article 14 of the Istanbul Convention, in the EU Strategy on the Rights of the Child and in UNESCO’s International technical guidance on comprehensive sexuality education – is essential to prevent unwanted pregnancies, promote gender equality and protect against sexual violence.
3.19.
The EESC calls on the Member States to integrate comprehensive, age-appropriate and scientifically rigorous sexuality education, adapted to the needs of different groups, into school curricula and relevant EU programmes, to introduce monitoring and evaluation of these programmes and to ensure that healthcare professionals are trained to respect informed consent and women’s autonomy.
3.20.
The EESC stresses the particular vulnerability of ethnic and religious minorities; women who are migrants, come from disadvantaged socio-economic backgrounds or live in rural areas; and women with disabilities, lesbian and bisexual women, among others, when it comes to accessing the right to abortion, and emphasises the need for an intersectional approach.
3.21.
The EESC considers that sustainable financial support needs to accompany legislative changes to make the effective right to access abortion care a reality.
3.22.
It considers that, as stated by the European Parliament in its Resolution of 11 April 2024 (adopted by 336 votes to 163 with 39 abstentions), the right to abortion, and funding thereof, should be included in the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights  ( 6 ) .
3.23.
The EESC calls on the European Commission to take up this initiative and guarantee that the right to abortion is accessible and effectively available, drawing up a timetable to be implemented in the immediate term.
3.24.
The EESC believes that the European Commission needs to clarify the arrangements for EU funds to finance the exercise of this right, and for the financial support mechanisms for civil society organisations that provide funds to women wishing to have an abortion.
3.25.
Given the current lack of data, the EESC recommends that the EIGE and Eurostat collect disaggregated data on sexual and reproductive rights.
3.26.
The EESC also calls on the EU to actively combat disinformation on abortion driven by the extreme right, which is a barrier to women’s autonomy and health and the exercise of their sexual and reproductive rights.
3.27.
The EESC condemns the backsliding on women’s rights and all regressive attempts to restrict or eliminate existing protection for sexual and reproductive health and rights and equality between women and men.
3.28.
The EESC recognises the fundamental role played by civil society, and in particular feminist and women’s rights organisations, in defending the right to abortion – especially in countries where abortion is prohibited or access is restricted – and in ensuring access to abortion by influencing legal reform, service provision and public education. The EESC calls for specific funding to support these organisations, especially in Member States where civic space is shrinking and the right to abortion is under threat.
3.29.
In addition, it urges the Member States and EU institutions to ensure legal, physical and online protection against stigmatisation, harassment and intimidation of activists, healthcare professionals and women who decide to abort.
3.30.
The EESC notes with great concern the global backsliding in the area of international support for family planning and sexual and reproductive rights. The United States Agency for International Development (USAID) has historically been one of the world’s largest funders of family planning and reproductive health services, supporting millions of women and girls worldwide. However, it has abolished almost all family planning subsidies and reinstated the global gag rule. The EESC urges the EU to step up its global leadership in upholding sexual and reproductive rights and to ensure access to vital care.
3.31.
The EESC therefore highlights and welcomes the work of the My Voice, My Choice movement on the European Citizens’ Initiative in finding a pragmatic way to tackle securing access to women’s right to abortion in the EU. It reiterates that abortion is a fundamental right that is inseparable from many other rights, not just the right to health, and that the genuine and effective exercise of this right must be ensured through an intersectional approach.
Brussels, 21 January 2026.

title: Opinion of the European Economic and Social Committee – Industrial Cooperatives: a tool for the challenge of inclusive and sustainable competitiveness (own-initiative opinion)
text:
Official Journal of the European Union
EN
C series
C/2026/868
27.2.2026
Opinion of the European Economic and Social Committee
Industrial Cooperatives: a tool for the challenge of inclusive and sustainable competitiveness
(own-initiative opinion)
(C/2026/868)
Rapporteur :
Giuseppe GUERINI (IT, III)
Co-rapporteur :
Michal PINTÉR (SK, Cat. 1)
Advisors
Diana DOVGAN (to the group III rapporteur)
Alexandra ŠARINOVÁ (to the category 1 co-rapporteur)
Plenary Assembly decision
23.1.2025
Legal basis
Rule 52(2) of the Rules of Procedure
Section responsible
Consultative Commission on Industrial Change (CCMI)
Adopted in section
12.9.2025
Adopted at plenary session
3.12.2025
Plenary session No
601
Outcome of vote
(for/against/abstentions)
198/0/3
1.    Conclusions and recommendations
1.1.
The European Economic and Social Committee (EESC) recommends that EU institutions, Member States and regional authorities integrate cooperative business education into mainstream entrepreneurship and vocational training at both secondary and tertiary level. This includes awareness campaigns and workshops targeting financial institutions and industry associations, ensuring they recognise the cooperative model. National and regional authorities should promote cooperatives among start-ups and young entrepreneurs. Specific opportunities for cooperatives should be included in the Erasmus+ programme.
1.2.
The EESC emphasises that EU institutions and Member States should recognise industrial cooperatives as key drivers of the European economy and implement targeted financial incentives (tax breaks, grants, low-interest financing) to encourage industrial cooperatives to adopt industrial symbiosis and circularity. Municipal and regional authorities should provide localised tax incentives and subsidies for newly established cooperatives, supporting economic development at community level.
1.3.
The EESC encourages national and regional investments in shared industrial parks and eco-industrial zones, to facilitate cooperative localisation. Additionally, cooperative knowledge-sharing platforms should be supported, enabling industrial cooperatives to exchange expertise and scale sustainable industrial production.
1.4.
The EU cohesion programmes should entail cooperative-specific policy measures to fully leverage the strength of cooperative businesses. Member States and the European Commission should incorporate cooperative-specific measures into regional development plans, ensuring industrial cooperatives are recognised as drivers of local sustainability. Cohesion funding, infrastructure investment plans and national strategies for underdeveloped regions should prioritise cooperative-led initiatives to enhance regional resilience.
1.5.
The growing importance of artificial intelligence and machine learning in the industry makes access to and storage and management of data essential and strategically important. For this reason, data-driven cooperatives will gain increasing importance in the management of industrial transformations. In this connection, the EESC encourages the European Commission and the Member States to support business associations, including cooperatives, in order to take collective initiatives to develop mutual organisations of this kind for the management and exchange of data.
1.6.
EU policies should recognise that the cooperative model offers distinct added value compared to conventional commercial enterprises by prioritising democratic governance, equitable distribution of wealth and strong community engagement, as well as its contribution to reinforcing EU strategic autonomy and its inherent resilience and adaptability, which are particularly well-suited to navigating complex social and economic challenges.
2.    Introduction and context
2.1.
The United Nations has proclaimed 2025 the International Year of Cooperatives (IYC2025) with the theme ‘Cooperatives Build a Better World’ and this choice originates from a growing recognition on the part of international institutions of the role played by cooperatives in many sectors.
2.2.
Co-operatives are, among the entities of the social and solidarity economy, the most structured form in entrepreneurial terms and the most widespread globally in terms of legal forms and identity principles. The European Union and many international institutions have recognised the decisive role played by social economy enterprises.
2.3.
The majority of cooperatives are SMEs, but many are also larger enterprises operating in the most competitive sectors. At least 12 % of the global population are members of cooperatives; two hundred and eighty million people work in cooperatives, from which they draw their main source of income and livelihood. In Europe, cooperatives represent 141 000 members, five million employees, and 250 000 enterprises  ( 1 ) .
2.4.
The European Union has recognised in its industrial strategy a specific ecosystem defined as the social and proximity economy. However, with this own-initiative opinion we wish to highlight that the cooperative model has been able to build competitive and successful companies and that their success is also based on their inclusive capacity, worker participation and constructive interaction with local communities.
2.5.
Industrial cooperatives play a crucial role in job creation and economic resilience, fostering inclusive business models. By aligning economic interests with environmental and social sustainability, cooperatives maintain resilience in the face of global challenges. Their ability to balance profitability, competitiveness and social responsibility makes them vital to Europe’s long-term economic strategy.
3.    European competitiveness and cooperatives
3.1.
Diversity of enterprise is recognised by the Treaty and the specificities of the cooperative model have recently been acknowledged by the European Court of Justice (Judgement of the Court (First Chamber) of 8 September 2011 – Joined Cases C-78/08 to C-80/08)  ( 2 ) , which legitimises targeted policies.
3.2.
The cooperative business model is fully in line with the values of the EU Treaty and the aims of the European Competitiveness Compass. In pursuing both economic and social objectives, cooperatives are an indispensable part of the ‘social market economy’.
3.3.
The cooperative enterprise form is not well known among citizens, the business community, banks and public administration. In some countries, cooperatives suffer from discriminatory practices and/or negative connotations and are not recognised as fully-fledged enterprises in the same way as conventional companies, adding extra obstacles to their growth and making it very difficult for them to access finance via traditional lending instruments. This opinion can contribute to disseminating the image of cooperatives as profitable businesses, generating value and wealth like conventional companies. The difference lies in how the wealth is distributed and the value put back into society.
3.4.
Cooperatives have a long-term objective of achieving economic and social sustainability through empowering people, anticipating changes and optimising the use of resources. Their profits are not used to maximise the remuneration of capital but to distribute benefits towards sustainable investment. During growth cycles, profits in profit-oriented businesses tend to be distributed in very generous dividends or bonuses. In contrast, in cooperatives profits are saved to better adapt to future shrinking cycles.
3.5.
The flexibility, adaptability and creativity of the cooperative method has permitted cooperatives to operate in all sectors of the economy and to adapt to emerging economic and societal needs. They are characterised by different sizes and different typologies. Industrial cooperatives, most of them being worker cooperatives, are not as well known. They are mainly active in manufacturing, construction or professional, scientific and technical activities. Industrial cooperatives are present in both traditional and emerging industrial sectors. Cooperatives also operate in education, health, services, agrifood, finance, etc., but also in disruptive sectors such as IT, software development, AI and biomedicine.
3.6.
Cooperatives, by their very nature, strive to empower all members equitably, making equality both a goal and a measure of their success. They have shown deliberate efforts and commitment to also apply these values in the workplace. For instance in worker cooperatives, workers’ involvement in the control and the management of enterprises leads to increased worker satisfaction, upskilling and productivity. The integration of social conditionalities into public procurement processes is vital for cooperatives, as it recognises and values their social mission alongside economic performance.
3.7.
Almost a million manufacturing jobs have been lost over the last four years in the EU  ( 3 ) , and cooperatives should be promoted as one way of counteracting deindustrialisation, to help the sector in ensuring just and fair twin transitions and to protect and create quality jobs. In this context reindustrialisation of Europe is a priority.
3.8.
Social cooperatives play an important role in the restructuring process and have been a driving force of social innovation. Work integration social cooperatives have a key role in bringing the most excluded workers to the labour market through effective and appropriate training. In some countries, such as Bulgaria, social cooperatives are major employers of people with disabilities.
3.9.
While industrial cooperatives have to meet carbon reporting requirements like any other enterprise, current reporting frameworks often fail to reflect their specific governance structures and social objectives; therefore, reporting systems should be adapted to better account for the cooperative model’s distinctive characteristics and contributions to sustainability.
3.10.
Many cooperative are engaged in or leading the digital and green transition, even in advanced sectors such as research on energy production from hydrogen, where for example in Italy a cooperative which originated in a university spin-off, has become a point of reference for innovation in the energy field. In Catalonia, a renewable energy cooperative counts almost 86 000 members and generates 71,11 GWh/year.
3.11.
The cooperative model has also proven to be effective and interesting in the management of water with functions of general interest. This has emerged from the work of the Alliance of Community-Owned Water Services in Europe (ACOWAS-EU), established during the consultation period for the 2020 recast of the EU Drinking Water Directive, which has shed new light on local community-owned drinking water supplies through cooperatives.
3.12.
For example, water cooperatives are managed and owned by local communities and, while interesting experiences have occurred in Austria, Denmark, Finland, Spain and Ireland, these are little known and little studied.
3.13.
In the renewable electricity sector, while Europe is currently undergoing a significant transition in its energy system shifting from centralised to decentralised production, a large part of the renewable energy communities are managed in cooperative forms. Energy cooperatives can supply energy from renewable resources at a lower price. If this model is promoted, European industry could be more competitive thanks to reduced energy costs for enterprises and the transition to a green economy could be faster.
3.14.
Cooperative banks play a vital role strengthening Europe’s regional economies, enhancing its financial and capital markets, fortifying its strategic autonomy globally, and financing Europe’s sustainable and just transitions.
3.15.
There are also cooperatives that bring together companies and organisations with common objectives into specialised clusters to maximise cooperation, innovation and socio-environmental impact. Each cooperative cluster is dedicated to a specific sector and supports its member cooperatives in facilitating access to their products or improving their management practices.
3.16.
Cooperatives serve as a crucial mechanism for addressing market failures by prioritising collective decision-making and equitable resource distribution, ensuring essential goods and services remain accessible despite economic downturns. They empower workers and stabilise employment in volatile industries. By reinvesting profits and focusing on long-term sustainability rather than short-term shareholder returns, cooperatives create resilience in unstable markets.
3.17.
In recent years, startups have increasingly embraced cooperative models, as shared ownership fosters open innovation and fair profit-sharing. These modern start-up cooperatives leverage digital tools to decentralise decision-making, making them both adaptable and competitive in emerging industries. The principle of inter-cooperation enables cooperatives to work together on joint projects, mutualise, obtain economies of scale and exchange knowledge; in combination with digital tools it provides a crucial competitive advantage.
4.    Cooperative contribution to shared prosperity and the EU’s inclusive industrial competitiveness
4.1.
One of the most interesting and successful practices for industrial restructuring and job preservation is the Workers Buyout (WBO), or business transfer to employees under the cooperative model.
4.2.
A WBO involves a restructuring process in which employees buy most or all ownership shares in their company and, in effect, become the co-owners. Most often, this occurs as an effort to rescue their companies from closure and to save jobs.
4.3.
A WBO can also serve as a tool to deal with transition and succession challenges in ‘healthy’ businesses, usually family-owned SMEs. This is primarily seen in France, where ‘the reasons for WBOs are not necessarily and even rarely related to a lack of economic performance’. The survey  ( 4 ) also notes: ‘it can be due to (owners’) retirement age or willingness to address a career change’.
4.4.
Despite the positive socio-economic impact of WBOs on saving jobs, know-how/skills and income within Europe, significant obstacles to WBOs should be emphasised: regulatory gaps, lack of appropriate legal and support measures, financing mechanisms, lack of a leveraged WBO model, limited interest from commercial banks, lack of awareness of the cooperative model among professionals dealing with liquidations and transfers. Nevertheless, technical assistance, including advisory services, training for future workers-owners and financial instruments are provided by cooperative federations and play a key role in guaranteeing the success of WBOs and limiting risk for workers. Member States should make greater use of ESF+ grants to support advisory services and technical assistance for WBOs.
4.5.
Additional measures supporting WBO should be implemented: direct financial mechanisms helping workers invest in enterprises in crisis or without successors; cooperative federations’ capacity to increase interventions in equity and quasi-equity and create specific guarantees; financial intervention from regional authorities completing workers capital and cooperative financial interventions; tax incentives for WBOs; preferential rights for workers in order to give them the best conditions for a takeover bid for an enterprise facing closure.
5.    Impact on jobs, education, skills, transition and technology
5.1.
Cooperative entrepreneurship generates more jobs than traditional entrepreneurship. For example, in Spain, out of 3 207 580 companies more than half of them (53,6 %) have no employees at all. In contrast, only 21,21 % of cooperatives do not have employees (mainly operating in construction and trade). Furthermore, 35,55 % of cooperatives have between one and two employees, exceeding the 27,99 % of traditional businesses, while another 19,08 % employ between three and five employees, compared to 9,65 % for the remaining businesses  ( 5 ) . Even though these figures may vary from country to country, they describe a general tendency to demonstrate a stronger focus on job creation and retention within the cooperative model.
5.2.
Draghi’s report on competitiveness recognises the need to close the skills gap in strategic industries. The cooperative principle ‘Education, training and information’ appeals to cooperatives to provide education and training for their members and employees. They are characterised by lifelong learning, thus enabling workers to respond with agility to changes.
5.3.
The International Cooperative Alliance, in its Cooperative Principles, defines a concern for community as one of the main values guiding the existence and operation of cooperatives: ‘Cooperatives work for the sustainable development of their communities through policies approved by their members’. This underlines that cooperatives are uniquely positioned to support local development and the triple transition (green, digital, circular), because their community-oriented, sustainable approach to business aligns with circular economy principles.
5.4.
Industrial cooperatives have the potential to drive the development of community-based economy, contributing to the bottom-up development of EU-wide clean and inclusive industries. Therefore, we encourage EU institutions to fully recognise the role that cooperatives can play in the implementation of new Clean Industrial Deal initiatives.
5.5.
The growing importance of artificial intelligence and machine learning in the industry makes access to and storage and management of data essential and strategically important. For this reason, data-driven cooperatives will gain increasing importance in the management of industrial transformations. Establishing cooperatives to manage and exchange data would serve the interests of people (workers, consumers, entrepreneurs) and SMEs which would not be in a position to access or process large amounts of data on their own.
5.6.
Cooperatives indeed seem particularly well suited for managing intermediary activities and data exchange or sharing between enterprises. Cooperatives in particular would enable the data management interests of the data subjects and the cooperative data holder – which in this case would be owned by the same data subjects – to coincide, and thus such structures would allow for participatory governance shared between citizens, companies and entrepreneurs.
5.7.
Industrial cooperatives can leverage their localised relationships to engage in industrial symbiosis, whereby the waste or the by-products of one industry or industrial cooperative can serve as production inputs for another. This supports resource efficiency and waste, energy, water and material savings. To support industrial cooperatives in adopting these practices, EU and national institutions should consider specific policies: locally-implemented or municipal tax incentives, tax breaks for newly-established cooperatives, subsidies, grants or other low-interest financing, support for regional knowledge-sharing platforms, as well as municipal and regional investments in infrastructure (such as shared industrial parks, eco-industrial zones, waste processing/recycling sites, reverse logistics hubs, etc.).
5.8.
Industrial cooperatives can play a specific role in regional development by fostering inclusive economic growth. Their democratic governance ensures that profits are re-invested locally, strengthening regional economies, social cohesion and employment. By prioritising long-term sustainability, cooperatives promote the resilience of local industries and encourage local and regional innovation in industry. This should be recognised in EU policies, including the cohesion funds, tailored funding and local or regional-level incentives, contributing to regional and local growth, employment and development.
5.9.
Among the challenges identified by cooperatives themselves is the issue of lacking cooperative knowledge. We encourage EU institutions, including the European Committee of the Regions, as well as national actors to prioritise mainstreaming education about the cooperative model in business education and ensure exposure of apprentices, learners in general and students and youth to cooperative principles and operations. In particular, the Erasmus+ programme should be more systematically leveraged in this field. The Erasmus+ programme should support vocational education and training (VET) in the cooperative business model. This could include the development of dedicated traineeships and mobility opportunities within cooperative enterprises across the EU.
5.10.
Specific attention should be paid to the development of cooperative knowledge in tertiary education to allow students to make an informed choice about cooperative entrepreneurship as a career option. Enhanced focus should be placed on promoting the cooperative model among start-ups and young entrepreneurs. The cooperative model should be promoted in the future EU start-up scale-up strategy.
5.11.
Cooperative business education should be integrated into the training activities of national and local business support organisations to enhance the attractiveness of the sector for business development. Dissemination of information is also important among the general public and among the private sector (banks, financial institutions, but also public administration), as well as within industry/business associations.

title: Opinion of the European Economic and Social Committee – Labour rights for journalists and media professionals as a safeguard for independence and truthful information (own-initiative opinion)
text:
Official Journal of the European Union
EN
C series
C/2026/867
27.2.2026
Opinion of the European Economic and Social Committee
Labour rights for journalists and media professionals as a safeguard for independence and truthful information
(own-initiative opinion)
(C/2026/867)
Rapporteur :
José Antonio MORENO DÍAZ
Co-rapporteur :
Christian MOOS
Advisor
Ricardo GUTIÉRREZ (rapporteur’s advisor, Group II)
Julian PLOTTKA (co-rapporteur’s advisor, Group III)
Plenary Assembly decision
23.1.2025
Legal basis
Rule 52(2) of the Rules of Procedure
(own-initiative opinion)
Section responsible
Employment, Social Affairs and Citizenship
Adopted in section
6.11.2025
Adopted at plenary session

Plenary session No
601
Outcome of vote
(for/against/abstentions)
209/4/11
1.    Conclusions and recommendations
1.1.
The environment in which journalists in Europe operate is becoming increasingly hostile. This is a threat to citizens’ right to reliable, pluralist and independent information. Faced with the democratic risk posed by the growing insecurity of journalists, public authorities must take urgent protective measures.
1.2.
The European Economic and Social Committee (EESC) welcomes the entry into force of the European Media Freedom Act (EMFA) and calls on the European Commission to ensure its full application by the Member States.
1.3.
The dominance of US Very Large Online Platforms, which capture 80 % of digital advertising revenue, threatens the sustainability of the European media sector. The EESC, therefore, calls upon the European Commission and the Member States to establish independent support for media outlets, in addition to existing subsidies. These measures could include a VAT reduction.
1.4.
The EESC is also concerned that concentration processes in the sector can undermine media pluralism in Europe. The EESC therefore calls upon the European Commission to use its competences in the area of competition law to guarantee competition, and therefore media pluralism, in the sector.
1.5.
The EESC calls for a considerable increase of funds for the protection of a sound information ecosystem, which can ensure satisfactory working conditions for journalists.
1.6.
In particular, the EESC calls on the European Commission to put forward an ambitious package with policy measures and investments to support quality jobs in the media sector.
1.7.
The EESC calls on governments to promote social dialogue and collective bargaining for all journalists, including freelancers, through the transposition of the Directive (EU) 2022/2041 of the European Parliament and of the Council  ( 1 ) on adequate minimum wages where applicable and the Guidelines on the application of Union competition law to collective agreements of solo self-employed persons  ( 2 ) . It further calls on the European Commission and Member States to fight bogus self-employment.
1.8.
The EESC calls on employers in the media sector to apply the EU Framework Council Directive 89/391/EEC  ( 3 ) . More efforts are needed to fully and effectively apply its provisions and the provisions of the related directives on the ground  ( 4 ) , as highlighted at the occupational safety and health (OSH) stock-taking summit in 2023  ( 5 ) .
1.9.
The EESC calls on the European Commission to follow up on the Recommendation on the Protection, Safety and Empowerment of Journalists  ( 6 ) , taking into account the assessment of the Study on Putting in Practice by Member States  ( 7 )
. The EESC stresses the need for deeper engagement with journalists’ organisations, to build structures that can safeguard journalists’ safety.
1.10.
Journalists are workers who are significantly exposed to stress, burnout, online harassment and digital overload. Precariousness, long working hours, deadlines and work-life imbalance can have a direct impact on health. The EESC has earlier stated that it would be useful for the Commission to consider how to follow up on the European Parliament resolution of 10 March 2022 calling for a directive on psychosocial risks to be adopted. The EESC is ready to issue an opinion on this matter  ( 8 ) .
1.11.
The EESC calls on the European Commission to monitor the application of the EU's legislative framework on the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in order to secure a fair balance between giving AI providers access to European data and ensuring the protection of journalists.
1.12.
The EESC encourages journalists’ unions and media organisations to address issues related to the use of AI in newsrooms within the framework of social dialogue, in order to ensure that AI serves the factual production of news, protects press freedom, and sustains jobs.
1.13.
The EESC calls on the European Commission to set a funding scheme for projects that develop the AI literacy of journalists. The Commission should consider possibilities to co-fund ‘European Journalism Academies’, which offer dual training for journalists and see whether it would be possible to subsidise for the period of training part of the salaries for young journalists from media companies that meet high standards concerning quality journalism and working conditions.
2.    General comments
2.1.    Introduction and background
2.1.1.
The journalism profession in Europe is under intense pressure. In addition to a decline in press freedom, the violations of which (physical violence, intimidation, judicial harassment, hostile legislation, etc.) are documented by the Council of Europe  ( 9 ) and European Union  ( 10 ) platforms, journalists are also faced with ‘deplorable working conditions in most EU Member States’, as the MPM2025 report  ( 11 ) attests. Research outlines that journalism’s ability to hold the powerful to account is diminishing: ‘Journalism, in its current trajectory, does not fulfil its Fourth Estate or “watchdog” function, and critically, this influences people’s understanding of society  ( 12 ) .’
2.1.2.
As stated in the annual report of the Council of Europe’s Platform for the Protection of Journalism, ‘in a democratic society, it is vital that journalists operate independently of political, commercial, or corporate influences. This independence hinges on the existence of decent working conditions, robust protections against legal threats, editorial autonomy from media owners and political entities, and the freedom for journalists to organise within trade unions or professional associations  ( 13 ) .’
2.1.3.
The Council of Europe’s Recommendation CM/Rec(2016)4  ( 14 ) underscores the importance of labour and employment laws in protecting journalists from arbitrary dismissal, reprisals and precarious working conditions that may subject them to undue pressures and ethical compromises. However, the 2025 Media Pluralism Monitor  ( 15 ) highlights institutional neglect in addressing precarious conditions in most EU Member States.
2.1.4.
According to the MPM2025  ( 16 ) , only 7 of the 34 European countries analysed – Denmark, Germany, Belgium, Estonia, Finland, the Netherlands, and Sweden – provide good working conditions for journalists. ‘The working conditions of journalists are deplorable in most EU Member States, with low salaries and weak or absent social security schemes,’ the report states.
3.    Background to the opinion
3.1.    Initiative against abusive litigation targeting journalists and rights defenders
In this opinion  ( 17 ) , the EESC points out that journalists are the most vulnerable to threats posed by strategic lawsuits against public participation (SLAPP). Limited in scope, the anti-SLAPP directive provides only a very partial response to these threats.
3.2.
Securing media freedom and diversity in Europe
In this own-initiative opinion  ( 18 ) , the EESC points out the increased social insecurity of journalists and their vulnerability to SLAPPs.
3.3.    Employment status
3.3.1.
According to the latest statistics  ( 19 ) , there are at least 400 000 journalists in EU Member States, representing 0,2 % of total EU employment. Freelance journalists account for between 20 % and 30 % of the total  ( 20 ) . Freelance journalists continue to be among the most vulnerable practitioners in the sector  ( 21 ) . However, growing insecurity also affects employed journalists: the number of collective agreements, particularly at the sectoral level, is tending to fall  ( 22 ) .
3.3.2.
In certain countries, the status of freelancer is misused by media outlets to minimise costs and responsibilities towards their workers  ( 23 ) . False self-employment is an increasing problem in the sector in some countries, as these journalists lack social security, such as sick leave, paid maternity and pension  ( 24 ) .
3.3.3.
One of the few countries where working conditions for freelancers have improved is the Netherlands, where the collective labour agreement increased journalists’ salaries, including the fees of freelancers working for major newspapers.
3.4.    Job insecurity
3.4.1.
Journalism is known for creating a high emotional load and pressurised working conditions  ( 25 ) . Evidence from OSHwiki shows that job insecurity is one a factor which can be linked to workers’ health and well-being. Workers who worry about the continuation of their jobs report stress, burnout and depression to a greater extent  ( 26 ) . As changes in the media landscape have led many media employers to cut staff, those who are left behind can be expected to pick up the work of their colleagues, which increases individual workloads. Journalist burnout is a significant issue according to an ETUI analysis  ( 27 ) and a recent European survey  ( 28 ) , with high percentages of journalists reporting mental health struggles and considering leaving the profession  ( 29 ) .
3.4.2.
Studies cited by research from the University of Limerick  ( 30 ) have shown that work is becoming more intense in newsrooms. The disruption caused by the digital transition is also reported as a concern, with many fearing that their jobs will be replaced by generative artificial intelligence  ( 31 ) . Cost-cutting measures have become a constant for many journalists, who are often faced with pay freezes, pay cuts and staff cuts  ( 32 ) .
3.5.    Working hours and work intensity
3.5.1.
National  ( 33 ) and European  ( 34 ) surveys have shown that a majority of journalists have had to take on extra duties and responsibilities, with most of them not receiving a commensurate pay rise. Work overload has become the norm: journalists often work on multiple stories with tight deadlines, which can lead to feelings of excessive pressure  ( 35 ) .
3.5.2.
Many freelancers have to take on non-journalistic work to make ends meet. A huge proportion of journalists have considered leaving journalism for a better-paid profession, making journalists’ careers shorter  ( 36 ) .
3.5.3.
Local and regional journalists are disadvantaged, frequently receiving lower salaries. Freelancers may have limited or non-existent access to social security schemes. Across all Member States, it is a trend that local media are more affected by the intertwining of decreasing advertising revenues and a biased allocation of state advertising and subsidies  ( 37 ) .
3.5.4.
The 2024 MPM report  ( 38 ) notes that negotiating collective agreements has become increasingly difficult. This makes journalists increasingly vulnerable ‘to external influences such as commercial or political pressures’  ( 39 ) .
3.5.5.
In France, unions have denounced the ‘uberization’ of young journalists, and media outlets resorting to the multiplication of short-term contracts, self-employment, payment in author rights, internships  ( 40 ) .
3.6.    Working relationship
3.6.1.
The intensification of work in newsrooms can lead to unacceptable behaviour. Bullying and harassment can happen, with significant consequences, including stress, depression, reduced self-esteem, self-blame and sleep disturbances  ( 41 ) . Sexual harassment can also occur. Studies have also highlighted the prevalence of burnout in the profession and increasing stress  ( 42 ) . Journalists most at risk of burnout are younger females with fewer years of experience, in small-circulation newspapers. A European survey reveals that 60 % of surveyed journalists report having experienced burnout  ( 43 ) .
3.7.    Third-party violence and online threats
Europe has seen an increase in incidents of violence against journalists  ( 44 ) . The latest MFRR Monitoring Report documented 1 548 press freedom violations targeting 2 567 media-related persons or entities in 2024  ( 45 ) .
3.7.1.
Journalists’ mental health can be affected by the exponential increase in online threats and attacks (harassment, intimidation, doxing, discreditation via fake accounts, etc.), which particularly target female journalists and journalists from minority backgrounds. At the end of 2023, the OSCE issued guidelines  ( 46 ) to help female journalists better cope with this new form of pressure. In 2024, the Council of Europe Platform  ( 47 ) identified new forms of digital attacks, with the use of deep fakes featuring journalists.
3.8.    Artificial intelligence
3.8.1.
AI both presents opportunities for journalists and threatens their role. Generative AI tools, like ChatGPT, pose a threat to journalists’ position, with many fearing they will be replaced by AI. In October 2024, OFF Radio Krakow in Poland faced controversy after replacing its human journalists with AI-generated presenters  ( 48 ) . An investigation by Belgian public broadcaster VRT News  ( 49 ) showed that more than half of the articles published in the fashion magazine Elle’s website were attributed to AI-generated journalists. AI models trained on large datasets of journalistic content may generate outputs that are very similar to copyrighted material, potentially leading to copyright infringement.
3.9.    Disinformation
3.9.1.
The massive spread of disinformation via social media, whether of foreign or domestic origin, forces journalists to be constantly on alert, including outside working hours. This pressure comes on top of the increased workload. The right to a better work-life balance and to be able to disconnect is seen as a new challenge. Some EU Member States have put legislation in place to allow workers to disconnect, as is the case in Denmark, Belgium, Ireland, Portugal, France, Spain and Italy  ( 50 ) .
3.9.2.
Reports reveal a growing loss of trust in the media, driven by the extent of misinformation. This loss of credibility has an impact on journalists’ morale and self-esteem. A survey found just 40 % of the respondents across the 47 surveyed markets say they trust most news  ( 51 ) . Faced with the poisoning of public debate by disinformation, many journalists feel powerless in the face of the threat that the profession could be stripped of its fundamental roles of accountability and oversight.
3.10.    Public service media
3.10.1.
Although they generally enjoy better working conditions and greater job stability, journalists in the public broadcasting sector are increasingly subject to financial restrictions, restructuring and political interference  ( 52 ) . Nearly half the EU Member States do not guarantee the governance and financial independence of their public service media (PSM)  ( 53 ) . Only 14 countries have fully independent public broadcasters: Sweden, Lithuania, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Belgium, Germany, Portugal, Denmark, Latvia, Finland, Ireland, Austria, Czechia and Estonia.
3.10.2.
The EESC calls on the European Commission to ensure a strict and timely implementation and enforcement of the European Media Freedom Act to ensure the managerial independence of PSM, as well as the long-term sustainability of its funding. Operational independence and sustainable funding have a direct impact on the working conditions of PSM journalists.
3.10.3.
The EESC supports the call of 14 EU Member States advocating for sustainable financial support for Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty and welcomes the decision for EU emergency support after the US government has halted its grant  ( 54 ) . RFR/RL can only play its crucial role of providing multi-lingual independent journalism to autocratic states if they aim to provide journalists with decent jobs and good working conditions.
3.11.    Self-censorship
3.11.1.
In a study commissioned by the Council of Europe  ( 55 ) , 37 % of survey respondents from the 47 member states of the Council of Europe and Belarus claimed that ‘unwarranted interference’ affected the way they went about their work, with self-censorship a highly prevalent theme. 69 % claimed that they had experienced psychological violence, mainly at the hands of public authorities. Psychological violence primarily included belittlement and humiliation by public authorities (48 %), intimidation by public authorities (56 %), threats of being hurt by public authorities (41 %) and slandering or smear campaigning by public authorities (43 %).

1.    Conclusions and recommendations
1.1.
The European Economic and Social Committee (EESC) recognises that permanent materials are fundamental to the circular economy. In this opinion, it focuses on their use in packaging and presents relevant policy recommendations. Permanent materials should be recognised in EU legislation in order to ensure that their unique contribution to circularity is reflected in future policy. The EESC considers it essential that the concept and characteristics of permanent materials be clearly recognised in the EU’s waste and resources framework, and that their role be acknowledged as conducive to the EU circular economy.
1.2.
The EESC supports the ambitious approach that the EU is adopting to achieve the 90 % separate collection target for packaging waste in all EU Member States by 2030, backed by targeted EU funding for advanced collection, sorting and high-quality recycling infrastructure. Stepping up separate collection is essential to enable closed-loop recycling and maximise the retention and value of permanent materials.
1.3.
The Committee proposes strengthening and harmonising extended producer responsibility (EPR) schemes across the EU Member States to actively incentivise the use of highly recyclable materials. This includes enforcing eco-modulated fees on the basis of clear criteria, ensuring transparent and proportional fee structures, ring-fencing revenues for reinvestment in the same material stream to drive genuine circularity outcomes and recognising other EPR best practices.
1.4.
The EESC notes that it is necessary to prioritise funding to accelerate investment in modern infrastructure for the separate collection, sorting and recycling of packaging waste. Special focus should be on regions with a lower performance or investment capacity, in order to ensure no Member State is left behind.
1.5.
The EESC recommends that the European Commission undertake a comprehensive assessment of EU citizens’ recycling behaviours, in order to identify deficiencies and best practices, and that it propose measures to enhance consumer participation in the separation of packaging waste as the essential first step of household recycling.
1.6.
It further recommends ensuring a socially sustainable transition to a circular economy by anticipating the impact on the labour market early and guaranteeing access to up-skilling and re-skilling to support job-to-job transitions, in order to ensure workers can fully benefit from and contribute to the evolving circular economy.
1.7.
The EESC recommends strengthening social dialogue at all levels and promoting collective bargaining, including at company level, to ensure workers are informed, consulted and involved in the shift towards circular business models, thereby reinforcing quality employment, workplace safety and social justice.
2.    General comments and background
2.1.
In the European Commission’s Political Guidelines for 2024-2029  ( 1 ) , Commission President Ursula von der Leyen sets out a vision for a more circular and resilient EU economy. The current European Commission – and the European Council, in its 2024-2029 Strategic Agenda  ( 2 ) – also prioritise helping the EU become more sustainable and keep resources within the EU economy for longer. The need to pay greater attention to circular economy goals raises specific questions, such as which materials are best suited to be used and kept in production within the circular economy and how can resources be managed sustainably. This own-initiative opinion aims to raise awareness of the concept of permanent materials , introducing policymakers, consumers and other stakeholders to key characteristics and considerations relating to the concept, and stimulating interinstitutional debate at EU level. Furthermore, it explores the potential mainstreaming of permanent materials in EU policy and legislation, especially ahead of the adoption of the Circular Economy Act, and promotes a regulation on waste that recognises the benefits of permanent materials for recyclability and circularity, focuses on harmonising circular economy policies, incentivises secondary materials and promotes sustainable product design.
2.2.
A permanent material can be defined as ‘a material whose inherent properties do not change during its lifecycles, regardless of the number of times it goes through a recycling process’. This is in contrast to other materials that degrade in the course of their use and recycling – each to a different extent. The inherent properties of steel, glass and aluminium, however, do not change during recycling and revert to their original characteristics, allowing for repeated recycling. Thus, we consider glass, aluminium and steel to be permanent materials and have selected them as the focus of this opinion. While permanent materials play an essential role in industrial applications, this opinion deliberately concentrates on their use in packaging, reflecting both the urgency and the opportunities in this domain. The packaging sector is undergoing significant regulatory reform through the Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation (PPWR), making it a timely and strategic entry point for mainstreaming permanent materials. Packaging waste remains one of the most visible and problematic waste streams at household level, with potential for further recycling increases. By focusing on packaging, this opinion addresses the part of the system where circularity breaks down, high-quality recycling being technically possible, yet constrained by logistics and human behaviour. Moreover, packaging is the primary interface between consumers and material use, offering a strategic space for aligning public behaviour, policy and investments. Scaling up the closed-loop recycling of glass, steel and aluminium packaging represents an immediate and impactful avenue for advancing the EU’s circularity goals.
2.3.
Permanent materials such as steel, aluminium and glass retain their inherent properties through multiple recycling loops, without degradation. Unlike materials that downcycle over time, permanent materials permit closed-loop material recycling, in which the recycled output can fully substitute virgin material for the same (or a similar) application multiple times. This intrinsic characteristic makes these materials uniquely suited to a truly sustainable and circular economy. The EESC emphasises the need to distinguish permanent materials from materials which downgrade over time, and it calls for the term ‘permanent materials’ to be mainstreamed in EU policy, legislation and circularity metrics. Recognising this category and implementing a targeted approach is essential to accelerate the EU’s climate and resource-efficiency goals.
2.4.
Permanent materials remain key resources for the circular economy and their repeated use and recycling can deliver benefits and savings. Tinplate, a cold-rolled flat steel product for packaging applications, is primarily produced via the basic oxygen furnace (BOF) route, with limited scrap input (15-20 %) due to strict quality requirements. Nevertheless, collected tinplate packaging consistently re-enters the steel cycle, substitutes for iron ore and coke in BOFs or serves as high-quality scrap in electric arc furnaces (EAFs). Tinplate recycling delivers meaningful resource, energy and CO 2 savings, while maintaining recycling rates above 80 % in several EU Member States  ( 3 ) . In the case of aluminium, recycling saves 95 % of the energy needed for primary production, as well as greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. In 2022, the carbon footprint of global primary aluminium production (from mine to cast house) was 15,1 tonnes of CO 2 equivalent (CO 2 e) per tonne, whereas the carbon emissions for recycled aluminium (gate-to-gate) were 0,52 tonnes of CO 2 e per tonne  ( 4 ) . For glass, on average, a 10 % increase in recycled glass (cullet) in the furnace decreases energy use by 3 % and CO 2 emissions by 5 %  ( 5 ) . The European Container Glass Federation (FEVE) lifecycle assessment shows that every tonne of recycled glass saves 670 kg of CO 2 (EU average, cradle-to-cradle). Melting 100 % cullet reduces CO 2 emissions by about 58 %, compared to a situation where no cullet is used  ( 6 ) .
2.5.
As the environmental, energy and water savings of recycling permanent materials are widely recognised, the value of permanent materials should be recognised in all relevant EU legislation, as should their role as key enablers of the EU’s climate and circularity goals. A circular, closed material loop, replacing virgin resources with recycled materials, helps reduce CO 2 emissions from aluminium, glass and steel production. Reducing Europe’s dependency on primary resources, achieving material sufficiency and scaling up collection and sorting infrastructure (especially in low-performing EU Member States) will support climate neutrality, and permanent materials will play a critical role in achieving these goals. These principles need to be anchored as the enabling pillars of an EU circular single market, supporting the broader EU objective of strategic autonomy, resilient EU supply chains and reduced reliance on third countries for raw materials.
2.6.
Despite the EU’s aim to double its circular material use rate by 2030, progress has been marginal, rising by around just one percentage point over more than a decade. Recycled material accounted for 11,8 % of material used in 2023, an increase of 1,1 percentage points from 2010. This shows that the EU is not currently on track to double its circular material use rate by 2030  ( 7 ) . The European Environmental Agency recommends increasing recycling and reducing reliance on primary resources to increase the circular material use rate  ( 8 ) , a task to which permanent materials are well suited.
3.    Specific comments: Scaling up the EU circular economy with permanent materials
3.1.
As the EU is still not on track to double its circular material use rate by 2030, stagnation in circularity metrics signals a deeper structural challenge. Europe continues to lose valuable resources to downcycling, exports and landfill disposal, undermining circularity, climate and competitiveness objectives. Without pro-circular systemic change , the EU risks falling behind on its green industrial leadership and weakening its resilience. Accelerating high-value, closed-loop material flows is essential to secure an EU circular economy that delivers environmental and strategic benefits.
3.2.
The EESC recommends shifting EU waste policy towards strategic resource management, keeping materials in circulation and prioritising high-quality, closed-loop recycling. The current definition of ‘recycling’ in Article 3(17) of the Waste Framework Directive (WFD) provides a general framework applicable to all materials. However, its application within the ‘waste hierarchy’ (Article 4 WFD) does not sufficiently distinguish between materials that are inherently circular, i.e. capable of being recycled multiple times without loss of function, and those that degrade with each cycle and are ultimately lost. Updating the hierarchy to better reflect this distinction would support the EU’s objective of enabling true circularity through multiple high-quality recycling loops, advancing the goal of a fully circular economy and maintaining stocks of these permanently available materials.
3.3.
The EESC calls for the concept and characteristics of permanent materials to be defined and recognised in the EU’s waste and resources acquis and asks that their role be acknowledged as being more appropriate to furthering the goals of the circular economy than that of materials which degrade over recycling cycles. This will help boost collection and recycling rates, reduce virgin-material dependencies and promote closed recycling loops, while eliminating waste and phasing out landfilling and incineration and associated resource loss.
3.4.
The PPWR introduces a forward-looking definition of high-quality recycling, acknowledging its specificity. Embedding a similar definition of high-quality recycling in the Circular Economy Act and the WFD would strengthen the EU’s legislative consistency and incentivise the efficient collection and sorting of materials that enable closed-loop material recycling. This would mark a strategic step towards fostering high-quality material retention and accelerating the circular transition. The EESC proposes including a definition in the WFD as follows: ‘high-quality recycling means any recycling process that produces recycled materials that are of equivalent quality to the original materials, based on preserved technical characteristics, and that are used as a substitute for primary raw materials for the same or other applications where the quality of the recycled material is retained. The recycled material can be recycled multiple times’.
3.5.
High-quality recycling of packaging depends on the availability of efficient separate collection and sorting systems. To enable true circularity, the EU should adopt a timely and ambitious approach towards achieving 90 % separate collection of packaging waste in all Member States by 2030. This effort should be supported by targeted EU funding for the development and use of innovative collection and sorting infrastructure, as well as by investment in high-quality recycling facilities, particularly in those EU Member States facing challenges in meeting EU recycling targets. Strengthening separate collection across the EU is a prerequisite for enabling closed-loop recycling and maximising the stock and value of permanent materials. In this context, the Multiannual Financial Framework 2028-2034, through the European Competitiveness Fund dedicated to the clean transition, should be aligned with circular economy objectives in order to fully leverage permanent materials.
3.6.
The success of any circular economy policy, particularly in the packaging sector, also depends on consumer behaviour. Consumers play a key role in initiating the recycling process through the correct separation and disposal of packaging waste at household level. Even the most advanced recycling technologies rely on this first step being done correctly. Greater efforts are needed, at both EU and Member State level, to raise awareness, provide clear and harmonised labelling, and ensure intuitive and accessible collection systems across all Member States. The EESC welcomes the Commission’s efforts to develop a harmonised EU-wide labelling scheme to help consumers make informed choices and sort their waste – especially packaging waste – correctly, meeting an essential condition for achieving high-quality recycling and closing material loops.
3.7.
Consumers are central to household waste recycling, as separating packaging waste is the essential first step. Their willingness depends on clear information, responsibility, quality education about recycling and circularity principles, labelling, motivation, incentives, facilitation and societal recognition of the practice. Industry, commerce, public authorities, legislators and the media must all contribute to creating supportive conditions. The Commission should investigate public attitudes across the EU in order to identify gaps and best practices for future strategies.
3.8.
To unlock the circular economy’s potential, its principles must be embedded in the EU single market. Enrico Letta’s 2024 report on the future of the single market highlights that a dedicated circular single market is essential to support environmental sustainability and drive innovation, competitiveness, resilience and growth. The report explicitly calls for the establishment of such a circular single market. Realising the vision requires policy actions, including the removal of regulatory fragmentation, barriers and national-level inconsistencies blocking the adoption of EU-wide circularity. Upholding core single market principles through the harmonisation, simplification and elimination of administrative burdens is critical for circular business models and a greater sense of ownership over sustainable practices. The EESC particularly emphasises the role of the Circular Economy Stakeholder Platform in furthering these goals.
3.9.
The EESC recognises that EPR schemes have been instrumental in achieving high collection and recycling rates for permanent materials. However, in line with an increased focus on circularity and recyclability, these must now evolve into truly strategic instruments that actively incentivise the use of permanent materials with high levels of recyclability and true circular potential. Article 8a of the WFD already calls for the modulation of EPR fees based on recyclability; however, this principle must be strengthened and enforced. Eco-modulated fees should not only consider whether a product can be recycled, but also whether it can be effectively collected, sorted and repeatedly recycled without a loss of material quality, thereby enabling it to substitute virgin resources. The EESC recommends aligning economic incentives with material performance and circularity outcomes via the effective establishment and reform of EPR schemes across the EU.
3.10.
The EESC recommends that general minimum requirements for EPR schemes be harmonised across the EU Member States and structured around the following principles:
—
transparent, proportional and non-discriminatory EPR fees, covering the net costs of collecting, sorting and recycling the specific packaging material for which they are paid;
—
ring-fencing of EPR revenues to ensure reinvestment in the collection and recycling of the same material stream, preventing cross-subsidisation across materials;
—
eco-modulation of fees, reflecting the actual recyclability of the packaging, its potential to be recycled multiple times without loss of intrinsic properties, and the real-world recycling rate of the material.
3.11.
Securing a reliable supply of, and improved access to, high-quality secondary raw materials (e.g. ferrous scrap, non-ferrous scrap and glass cullet) is essential. The EESC supports refining the EU’s end-of-waste criteria, improving data collection and quality for sustainability metrics, and aligning all relevant EU legislation to enhance the availability of secondary materials across the EU single market.
3.12.
Achieving high-quality recycling and material circularity across the EU will require targeted investment in infrastructure, particularly separate collection, sorting and recycling of packaging waste. Many EU Member States face structural and budgetary challenges in scaling up this infrastructure to meet EU targets. The EESC calls for a stronger focus within relevant EU funding instruments to support modern, high-efficiency collection and sorting infrastructure. Special attention should be given to regions with lower performance or investment capacity, in order to ensure no Member State is left behind.
3.13.
The EESC underlines that the transition towards a circular economy based on permanent materials must be socially sustainable. This requires placing workers and their rights at the centre of the process. As industries adapt to circular business models, early anticipation of labour market impacts – through forward-looking skills policies, job mapping and investment in vocational training (re-skilling, up-skilling) – is essential. Rights-based access to upskilling, including paid educational leave and job-to-job transition measures, must be guaranteed to ensure that workers can fully benefit from and contribute to the evolving circular economy.
3.14.
The EESC emphasises the key role of social dialogue and calls for the PPWR to be supported by a strong social pillar: not only raising awareness and monitoring company-level transitions, but also ensuring that workers are effectively informed, consulted and involved. It is of paramount importance, when implementing the PPWR, to secure smooth labour transitions, assess the impact of EU obligations, invest in quality job-creation and strengthen collective bargaining, health and safety, skills and social protection measures. Social dialogue, collective bargaining and worker involvement at all levels must be strengthened to ensure that greater circularity with permanent materials contributes to quality employment, health and safety at work, and social justice. At company and sector level, collective agreements can advance circularity by committing to greater use of secondary raw materials, design-for-recycling, and high-quality collection and recycling.
