1.    Conclusions and recommendations
1.1.
Regarding the commercial determinants of health, the European Economic and Social Committee (EESC) stresses the need to take a comprehensive, preventive approach based on fundamental human rights and the exposome concept. These determinants are defined as strategies and practices of private actors that negatively influence health and democratic checks and balances.
1.2.
The EESC reiterates the key role that the European Union (EU) and its Member States must play through ambitious policies, targeted action plans and strategic funding. In particular, the next Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) for 2028-2034 must prioritise health and the shift towards prevention as a pillar of European resilience, and also respond to health, social, economic, professional and environmental vulnerabilities aggravated by pandemics, multidimensional crises and structural inequalities.
1.3.
The EESC stresses that comprehensive consideration of all aspects of health is fully in line with economic imperatives, which can be linked to public health objectives and be seen as a general interest. As such, the EESC encourages a balanced framework for action that offers European businesses the necessary conditions to move towards more positive health models. By including the precautionary principle and transparency and due diligence clauses in public policies, the EU can better protect citizens’ health, but also unlock the innovation potential of European businesses and actively help the EU be a pioneer of the well-being economy, combining economic performance, social cohesion, health solidarity and sustainable prosperity.
1.4.
The EESC is prepared to support a competitive EU, not through a race to the bottom in terms of health or society, but by making Europe the leading continent for quality of life, a pillar of the European project.
1.5.
The EESC also draws attention to the need to guarantee a strong approach to health and safety at work, in line with Principle 10 of the European Pillar of Social Rights. There is an urgent need to strengthen existing frameworks to prevent occupational risks, in response to working environments and ways of working that have a negative impact on health. An approach focused on the quality of working conditions improves both the competitiveness of businesses and the well-being of workers, in the spirit of shared prosperity.
1.6.
The EESC highlights a number of European projects that illustrate the need to take action on commercial determinants of health, including strengthening European governance on low-value care, by integrating commercial determinants of health into the assessment of health systems, in line with the work of the European Commission’s Health Systems Performance Assessment (HSPA). The EESC endorses EuroHealthNet’s analysis on the need for strict regulation of industrial practices that encourage overconsumption of health care and products with no demonstrable benefit for patients. The EESC supports initiatives such as the PreventNCD Joint Action on the prevention of cancer and other non-communicable diseases (NCDs), which promote coordinated policies to regulate harmful industries, tax harmful products and limit marketing of them. It also encourages cross-cutting approaches, inspired by international models such as Canada, to include NCDs in all public policies and to guarantee a sustainable and equitable health system based on quality of care.
1.7.
The EESC calls for the professionalisation of the health workforce and investment in ethical and scientific training, as recommended in the joint roadmap of the World Health Organization (WHO) and the Association of Schools of Public Health in the European Region (ASPHER). Competent staff is essential to ensure preventive policies are effective.
1.8.
The EESC recommends strengthening the strategic role of the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) by extending its current mandate and resources beyond communicable diseases to include commercial determinants of health and NCDs with the aim of equipping the EU with a forward-looking and independent analytical capacity, commensurate with contemporary public health challenges. With this in mind, the EESC supports the creation of a European Observatory on Commercial Determinants of Health, as described in point 6.3, under the aegis of the ECDC and in coordination with other relevant agencies (the EMA, EU-OSHA, Eurostat, etc.).
1.9.
The EESC supports the funding allocated to health in the proposal for the 2028-2034 Multiannual Financial Framework, in particular through the Competitiveness Fund and the tobacco tax, but regrets the lack of a dedicated health programme, which makes health priorities less visible. The EESC calls for prevention, health education and strengthening health systems to be included in the national and regional partnership plan budgets (the NRPPs), with stronger governance to deal with the commercial determinants of health.
1.10.
The EESC stresses the crucial role that Member States could play, supporting a voluntary coalition of states promoting stricter regulation of aggressive marketing, including in the digital space.
1.11.
The EESC calls for the creation of a European healthy business label, issued on the basis of rigorous, independently verified criteria. This label would highlight businesses working to reduce the promotion of products that are harmful to health, maintain transparency in these sectors, and fund prevention campaigns, while at the same time regulating conflicting ‘healthwashing’ initiatives. Social and solidarity-based practices can be inspiring in this area.
1.12.
The EESC calls for the active and systematic involvement of civil society and patient organisations at all stages of the development, implementation and evaluation of health policies in the context of commercial determinants of health, both at European and international level. At the same time, it stresses the importance of a rigorous assessment of the financial links between patient organisations and industries that have an impact on health, making funding mechanisms more transparent. The aim of this approach is to analyse the impact of these links on public policies, in particular in authorisation, reimbursement and research procedures, while ensuring effective representation of citizens’ needs.
1.13.
The EESC recommends that the EU strengthen its role in global governance of public health, particularly in the work of the WHO, the G7, the G20 and the UN.
2.    An integrated approach to addressing determinants of health
2.1.
Health is a fundamental human right shaped by a complex set of social, economic, commercial, environmental and digital determinants. 70 % of the state of health is influenced by these factors, compared to only 10 % for individual behaviours. All environmental factors a person is exposed to throughout life and the impact they have on health are summarised by the exposome concept. The EESC encourages public policies based on a systemic approach that takes these determinants into account.
2.2.
NCDs – cardiovascular diseases, cancers, chronic respiratory diseases, diabetes – account for almost 90 % of deaths and 85 % of cases of incapacity in Europe. The EESC stresses the need to address their structural causes, in addition to prevention and access to care, to ensure better health for all.
2.3.
The EESC builds on the work of the WHO, in particular its study on commercial determinants of health  ( 1 ) , which defines these as the strategies of private actors to maximise their profits to the detriment of public health. The WHO calls for strict regulation, dissuasive taxation of harmful products and improved monitoring of harmful trade practices.
2.4.
Like digital platforms that drive disinformation, the tobacco, alcohol, agri-food and fossil energy industries have a considerable influence on public health, not only through the products they market, but also through their lobbying strategies, influence on scientific research and ability to influence public policies to their advantage.
2.5.
The EESC highlights the importance of multi-stakeholder and cross-sectoral cooperation. It is not enough to rely just on one tool: public policies need to be developed to transform living environments, reduce health-related social inequalities and redirect the influence of economic actors whose interests go against public health towards a well-being economy.
2.6.
As a model of a society that strikes a balance in which economic competitiveness and social well-being reinforce each other, the EU must adopt an integrated approach to regulating and preventing the negative impacts of the commercial determinants of health.
3.    Understanding the impact of commercial determinants
Documented analyses by international and European institutions
3.1.
The WHO has pointed to the commercial practices of certain industries that aggravate health and environmental impacts: aggressive marketing targeting children and vulnerable populations (80 % of advertising for ultra-processed food targets young people), the influence of biased industrial funding on research (e.g. covering up the dangers of tobacco), intensive lobbying (mobilising significant resources to prevent the adoption of public policies that would benefit the population), externalisation of the costs of diseases to society and strategies to shift responsibility (for example, falsely promoting e-cigarettes as less harmful).
3.2.
According to the latest available estimates  ( 2 ) , cardiovascular diseases, obesity, alcohol and tobacco result in major economic and health costs estimated at over EUR 700 billion per year for European health systems, with tobacco (700 000 deaths, EUR 98-130 billion, as much as 1,39 % of GDP), alcohol (255 000 deaths, EUR 125 billion), obesity (over EUR 10 billion in healthcare costs) and spending by harmful industries (e.g. EUR 30 million to curb sugar taxes) having specific impacts. Harmful substances (tobacco, alcohol, ultra-processed food) cause around 2.7 million deaths per year in Europe, or 25 % of total mortality (approximately 7 400 deaths per day).
3.3.
The EESC reiterates that occupational safety and health, enshrined in Principle 10 of the European Pillar of Social Rights, remains a priority. Workplace absences due to chronic diseases and psychosocial risks represent a cost of around 2,5 % to 4 % of EU GDP, or between EUR 470 and 750 billion per year, according to studies that include the direct and indirect costs  ( 3 ) .
3.4.
The EESC stresses the importance of prevention in relation to neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson’s, advocating stepping up assessment of the risk factors, scientific independence and the precautionary principle  ( 4 ) .
3.5.
The WHO  ( 5 ) highlights the fundamental link between public health and economic stability, promoting interconnected policies and modelling tools.
4.    Fostering a virtuous circle for European businesses
4.1.
Far from being a hindrance to competitiveness, a shift towards healthy and responsible commercial practices is a major opportunity for European companies. By moving away from harmful products and integrating prevention of NCDs into their business models, companies can not only reduce regulatory and reputational risks, but also stimulate innovation and become more attractive to consumers and investors.
4.2.
The development and uptake of healthier and sustainable products can lead to a virtuous circle in which companies benefit from more stable regulations, increasing demand for responsible alternatives and alignment with societal expectations for public health. However, like greenwashing, healthwashing is a real risk. A reliable European ‘healthy business’ certification based on clear and rigorous criteria is therefore needed. The EU and its Member States could promote responsible innovation through tax incentive schemes and in public procurement.
4.3.
By ceasing to rely on marketing risky products, and investing in innovative alternatives, companies can not only anticipate regulatory developments but also become more competitive in the long term. Public health innovation – products, services, consumption patterns – is becoming a strategic lever for economic growth. At EU level, encouraging this transition is fully in line with the willingness to build competitiveness based on excellence, responsible innovation and sustainability, in a geopolitical context that requires enhanced health sovereignty, industrial independence and social attractiveness.
Rethinking prevention as a strategic lever for the European Union
4.4.
The cost of prevention must not be seen as a commercial constraint or threat. On the contrary, it is a key investment lever, both in terms of the sustainability of health systems and the well-being of the population, which is a distinctive feature of the European model and its competitiveness. The EESC supports a system of targeted taxation on harmful products such as tobacco, alcohol and ultra-processed foods to finance preventative actions by health systems.
4.5.
A well-trained public health workforce is essential to tackle the commercial determinants of health in the EU. Without skills or ethics, prevention efforts, regulating harmful industries and implementing evidence-based policies will not be enough. The EESC supports the WHO-ASPHER roadmap to boost the capacity of the public health workforce, which is essential for the resilience of health systems, ethical governance and protection from commercial influences.
Creating a favourable ecosystem
4.6.
The EU has a strong interest in speeding up this transition to a sustainable health economy by providing financial incentives, a coherent regulatory framework and rigorous public-private partnerships in the food, pharmaceutical, digital and health sectors. By building an ecosystem conducive to social innovation and health, the EU can make the prevention of NCDs a real driver of growth and resilience. This approach also includes improving existing treatments and reducing preventable diseases, such as certain forms of cancer or Parkinson’s disease when detected and addressed at an early stage.
4.7.
In line with the protection of personal data, the EESC calls for greater transparency regarding the real purposes of the exploitation of health and consumer data, especially when it feeds advertising algorithms or behavioural optimisation tools. It is necessary to prohibit the use of health data that boosts harmful business models (algorithmic suggestion of ultra-processed or polluting products). The EESC calls for a strict framework for systems used to target audiences based on their medical or social fragility, as well as for platforms and companies to be labelled according to their level of ethical compliance (principle of ‘digital health responsibility’).
4.8.
Patient associations, which represent citizens’ experiences, and civil society organisations are key democratic actors that are essential for health democracy as well as social dialogue. To preserve this legitimacy, the EESC recommends ensuring an enabling and transparent environment that allows them to fully play their role as guardian, advocate and representative of the general interest in the development, implementation and evaluation of health policies.
5.    Taking actual experiences and claims into account
5.1.
The EESC stresses the importance of greater consideration of concrete experiences and recommendations from recent European initiatives. The report of the European Commission’s HSPA Group  ( 6 ) warns of the persistence of ‘low-value care’, i.e. medical interventions with no proven benefit, promoted by aggressive commercial strategies, to the detriment of quality of care and the financial sustainability of health systems. Similarly, the European EuroHealthNet and the global NCD Alliance  ( 7 ) call for stronger regulation of harmful industries (tobacco, alcohol, ultra-processed food) and warn about their capacity to influence public policies through lobbying and targeted marketing, including digital marketing. The EESC agrees with these findings and calls for more rigorous governance of commercial determinants of health.
5.2.
In line with this momentum, the EESC supports the PreventNCD Joint Action  ( 8 ) , a coordinated European initiative to integrate commercial determinants of health into policies for the prevention of non-communicable diseases. It sets out the key proposals of taxing harmful products, limiting marketing of them, creating independent regulations and strengthening European cooperation. Like Canada, which has implemented a health determinants map and a well-being economy plan, the EESC calls on the EU to have a similar framework for cross-cutting action. It recommends the adoption of a comprehensive European strategy to combat the commercial determinants of health, anchored in the fairness, prevention and the resilience of public systems.
6.    Towards a stronger European framework for the well-being economy
6.1.
In the face of the challenges posed by commercial determinants of health, the EU must put in place an ambitious and structured well-being framework that includes health as a fundamental pillar of public policies. This requires a comprehensive approach that combines strengthened governance, monitoring commitment from companies, economic incentives and international cooperation.
6.2.
Applying the precautionary principle in all commercial and industrial policies that affect health:
—
the EU must incorporate the precautionary principle into its economic, social and commercial decisions in order to anticipate the harmful effects of industries on public health;
—
the EESC recommends a targeted application of the precautionary principle, avoiding an indiscriminate or generalised approach to all trade sectors. The aim is not to stigmatise an entire business ecosystem, but to concentrate regulatory efforts on industries whose products or practices have a proven, lasting and systemic impact on public health, such as tobacco and related devices (vapes, synthetic nicotine), alcohol and spirits (including through cultural marketing strategies), ultra-processed foods high in salt, sugar and trans fatty acids, digital platforms that promote a sedentary lifestyle, disinformation or overconsumption, chemical industries, pesticides and neurotoxic solvents (as highlighted in the case of Parkinson’s);
—
a systematic health impact assessment should be put in place before developing EU trade policies in these sectors, enabling heightened vigilance towards biased industrial financing.
6.3.
Extending the mandate and resources of the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC), such as coordination with other European agencies (the EMA for medicines, EU-OSHA for health at work):
—
the EESC proposes that the ECDC, which is currently focused on communicable diseases, extend its mandate and resources to include specific monitoring of commercial determinants of health and NCDs. This would include an observatory element that could collect data, analyse trends and make recommendations on prevention policies, in conjunction with the European Commission’s directorates-general. This would make it possible to sustainably anchor prevention of NCDs in the European Health Strategy, while ensuring better coordination of long-term responses;
—
the EESC calls for a three-fold approach – enhanced monitoring, consolidated regulation based on independent multi-factor assessments, coordination of national commitment – to ensure effective, coherent and resilient prevention at EU level.
6.4.
Incorporating prevention into the next European Multiannual Financial Framework:
—
The EESC takes note of the European Commission’s proposal regarding the 2028-2034 Multiannual Financial Framework and welcomes the funding for health provided for in the Competitiveness Fund and the creation of targeted own resources such as the tobacco tax to help finance prevention policies. However, the EESC regrets that the structure outlined does not include a dedicated health programme, which risks making European health priorities less visible and comprehensible. It calls for health – particularly in relation to prevention, health education and support for health systems – to be given a fundamental place in the future national and regional partnership plan budgets (the NRPPs).
6.5.
Creating a European ‘healthy business’ certificate and taking inspiration from the social and solidarity economy:
—
the social economy proposes economic models that favour the general interest and that fully incorporate health issues by bringing production and consumption models into line with NCD prevention and reduction objectives;
—
the creation of a European ‘healthy business’ certificate would allow recognition of and support for companies that are taking concrete actions, such as reducing the promotion of harmful products, supporting prevention campaigns, improving working conditions and the transparency of their sectors. However, in order to avoid adverse effects of certification, such as hiding behind it in the case of greenwashing, this certification will need to be based on a rigorous and independent verification system with demanding and evolving criteria.
6.6.
Bringing European policies into line with WHO and UN objectives:
—
the EU must take its fight against commercial determinants of health to an international scale, following the recommendations of global organisations on NCDs and bringing its policies in line with Sustainable Development Goal 3.4, which aims to reduce premature mortality due to NCDs.

title: Opinion of the European Economic and Social Committee – Evaluating the impact of public policies in the medium and long term through intergenerational budgeting (own-initiative opinion)
text:

16.1.2026
Opinion of the European Economic and Social Committee
Evaluating the impact of public policies in the medium and long term through intergenerational budgeting
(own-initiative opinion)
(C/2026/12)
Rapporteur :
Nicoletta MERLO
Advisor
Luciano MONTI (for the Group II rapporteur)
Plenary Assembly decision
23.1.2025
Legal basis

Section responsible
Employment, Social Affairs and Citizenship

3.9.2025
Adopted at plenary session

Plenary session No

Outcome of vote
(for/against/abstentions)

1.    Conclusions and recommendations
1.1.
This own-initiative opinion aims to promote the introduction of ‘intergenerational budgeting’ by encouraging an approach that would foster better awareness of how resources are allocated by EU, national and local financial programming to the different generations and in particular to young people. This should be done while fully respecting Member States’ competences and budgetary autonomy.
1.2.
The EESC calls on the Member States to systematically consider the intergenerational dimension in their budgets, for instance by applying the Youth Check to all relevant national budgetary items or through other methods, clearly identifying generational and potentially generational measures. This tool would help better align public spending with the principles of intergenerational fairness, while also promoting a generational exchange between young people and older people. Such an approach should also promote youth co-participation, especially for the detection of potentially generational measures.
1.3.
Once the key generational priorities and funding streams have been identified, the EESC encourages giving consideration to activating structured and meaningful youth participation as an integral part of budgetary planning and monitoring. In this regard, the Council has invited the European Commission, in accordance with the principle of subsidiarity, to ensure that young people’s voices are taken into account at all levels, with the introduction of the Youth Test/Youth Check at EU level, a youth impact assessment or other similar youth mainstreaming instruments  ( 1 ) .
1.4.
The EESC believes that, in order to promote intergenerational equity, Member States’ budgets should ensure a fair equilibrium between family and child per capita expenditure and old age per capita spending. For this reason, the EESC calls for consideration to be given to introducing a significant threshold for ‘families and children’ category expenditure within social protection budgets, ensuring that a set share of public resources is earmarked for ‘protection for youth’.
1.5.
The EESC highlights the importance of ensuring the long-term sustainability of social protection systems by conducting quantitative assessments on intergenerational fairness.
1.6.
In accordance with Article 322(1)(a)  ( 2 ) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU, which stipulates that the Parliament and the Council, acting through the ordinary legislative procedure and after consulting the Court of Auditors, are to adopt the financial rules that govern the procedure for establishing and implementing the budget and for presenting and auditing accounts, the EESC suggests that national and regional level intergenerational budgeting be introduced as part of the conditionality for the new 2028-2034 cohesion policy programming cycle and in the implementation of the new ‘national and regional partnership plans’. This would ensure long-term fiscal sustainability and strengthen the intergenerational equity of public spending.
2.    Context
2.1.
Economic, social and environmental crises affect different segments of the population asymmetrically, with particularly severe effects on the younger generations. As emphasised by the Commission  ( 3 ) , young people are among those most affected by economic and social crises, with a potentially lasting impact on their career prospects, well-being and trust in institutions. Almost half of young people reported emotional or psychosocial problems in the past year, with global events such as the COVID-19 pandemic and geopolitical crises contributing to heightened stress levels  ( 4 ) .
2.2.
The phenomenon of demographic ageing in Europe increasingly raises the issue of intergenerational equity, particularly as the steadily declining number of individuals under 30 face the risk of their interests being insufficiently represented in Member States’ policy-making. This risk is heightened by two factors: first, the percentage of the population in this age group is steadily decreasing; second, more than half of those under 30, specifically those under 18, do not represent an electoral constituency. While in the year 2000 individuals under 20 accounted for 23,7 % of the population, it is estimated that by 2030 they will make up only 19,2 %. This proportion is expected to decline steadily to 18,3 % in 2050, and to 17,8 % by 2100  ( 5 ) . A comparable decline can also be seen within the 15-24 age group, whose share of the population is projected to fall from 10,5 % in 2020 to 9,5 % in 2050  ( 6 ) , underscoring a broader demographic shift towards an ageing population. Conversely, the proportion of those over 65, which stood at 16,9 % in 2000, is projected to reach 26,1 % by the end of this decade.
2.3.
Demographic developments impact labour markets, pension and social protection systems and Europe’s geopolitical position in the world  ( 7 ) . Labour shortages exist in various sectors and occupations and will likely increase with the projected decline in the working age population from 265 million in 2022 to 258 million by 2030  ( 8 ) . As mentioned in the EESC opinion SOC/796, the old-age dependency ratio (i.e. the number of people aged 65+ per 100 people aged 15-64) is changing rapidly: this ratio is projected to increase from 33.3:100 in 2023 to 45.5:100 in 2040, and to 59.7:100 in 2100, which means that 59.7 retired people will depend on 100 people of working age.
2.4.
The data clearly show a need to ensure the sustainability of welfare systems: policies on pensions, health and social welfare should be structured in such a way as to avoid imbalances between generations. With Europe’s ageing population, if current policies do not provide for adequate investments in birth rates, youth employment and lifelong learning, the risk is that future generations will not have access to an appropriate level of social protection.
3.    General comments
3.1.
Political and budgetary choices influence the distribution of public resources. The Member States must repay the funding received through the RRF, while also supporting investments planned under the new ReARM plan, and this makes it essential to introduce measures and guarantees that prevent the burden from falling disproportionately on the younger generation.
3.2.
As the Commission President Ursula von der Leyen stated in her Mission Letter to the Commissioner for Intergenerational Fairness, Youth Culture and Sports, ‘the EU Commission must ensure that decisions taken today do not harm to future generations and ensure that the interests of present and future generations are respected throughout EU policy and law making’. Solidarity and intergenerational equity in access to resources should therefore be promoted. The Commissioner was tasked with developing a comprehensive Strategy on Intergenerational Fairness, supported by the Joint Research Centre (JRC), which has recently launched an EU Policy Lab to facilitate the strategy’s design  ( 9 ) . This initiative aims to avoid a ‘compartmentalised work’ approach by involving all DGs and envisages the collaboration and involvement of the European Youth Forum, the OECD, Age Platform Europe and other external stakeholders to co-create the strategy.
3.3.
As stated in the EESC opinion SOC/759  ( 10 ) , the EU should encourage the Member States to strengthen measures that address intergenerational unfairness and promote social justice, ensuring strong coordination for policy coherence. Additionally, the Member States should reinforce cross-sectoral policies benefiting young people and reducing generational divides. Several pilot schemes have been conducted in this field in the EU, resulting in scientific impact studies, monitoring studies  ( 11 ) and even ex post evaluations on draft laws for young people. Two EU countries – Austria and Germany  ( 12 ) – have carried out ex ante ( Jugend-Check ) and ex post evaluations that are particularly interesting, while the youth check is particularly developed in Italy at local level ( Valutazione di Impatto Generazionale   ( 13 ) ).
3.4.
The generational impact assessment of medium- and long-term policies should foster mechanisms for youth participation in public decision-making, ensuring that policies are formulated with the needs and expectations of the new generations in mind. Initiatives such as the Youth Test  ( 14 ) , introduced in some countries and promoted at EU level by the EESC, aim precisely at assessing the effect of new legislation on young people in advance, making policies more inclusive and future-oriented. Recent Council Conclusions  ( 15 ) invited the Commission, in accordance with the principle of subsidiarity, to ‘ensure that young people’s voices are taken into account at all levels, with the introduction of the youth check at EU level, a youth impact assessment or other similar youth mainstreaming instruments’. In this regard, the Commission has also embarked on a path of engaging younger generations through the EU Youth Dialogue  ( 16 ) and Youth Policy Dialogues initiatives.
3.5.
Conditionality regarding certain cross-cutting and thematic enabling conditions has already been adopted in the current 2021-2027 European cohesion policy cycle. Regulation (EU) 2021/1060, which lays down common provisions for the European Regional Development Fund, the ESF+, the Cohesion Fund, and other funds – and specifically Recital 21, Article 15 and, in particular, Annex III and IV thereof – sets out the current thematic enabling conditions required for the effective and efficient use of these funds. These include the presence of a national strategic framework for gender equality (enabling condition 4.2), as well as strategic policy frameworks in areas such as education and training, health, long-term care, and social inclusion (enabling conditions 4.3, 4.4 and 4.6). These enabling conditions apply to the current 2021-2027 programming period and form the baseline requirements for accessing EU cohesion funding under the existing regulatory framework  ( 17 ) . Conditionality is also required within the RRF  ( 18 ) .
4.    Specific examples of evaluation mechanisms
4.1.
The Commission’s discussion paper ‘The Intergenerational Dimension of Fiscal Sustainability’ provides a framework for assessing lifetime net tax contributions across generations by explaining how generational accounting works. It reveals that current EU fiscal policies place a disproportionate burden on future generations, with age-related spending (pensions, healthcare) projected to reach 20 % of GDP. The study adopts two key metrics: the intertemporal budget gap (IBG), which measures the adjustment needed to stabilise public debt over 50 years; and the Auerbach-Gokhale-Kotlikoff (AGK) indicator, which quantifies the fiscal imbalance between current and future generations. This analysis shows that future European newborns could face tax rates 2-3 times higher than current retirees, even if with the impact of pension reforms the impact of generational imbalances is significantly lower. The methodology described in this discussion paper is based on the allocation of government spending across different age cohorts, using statistical data and economic modelling. Public expenditure is classified into functional categories according to the statistics on income and living conditions (SILC) and classification of the functions of government (COFOG)  ( 19 ) framework, which ensures comparability across countries. To estimate the distribution of public spending by age, the report constructs age profiles for different spending categories, relying on administrative data, national accounts and projections from the Commission. The methodology involves identifying the primary recipients of public services, modelling spending patterns over the life-cycle and applying these distributions to demographic data (i.e. education spending is assigned primarily to younger age groups, healthcare costs increase with age and pension expenditures are allocated to older cohorts).
4.2.
The COFOG classification splits government spending into ten divisions from ‘01 - general public services’ to ‘10 - social protection’  ( 20 ) . In the manual, the ‘Assigning an appropriate function: case studies section analyses “Case 4 – Protection of Youth”. This case concerns the classification of government expenditure aimed at protecting and supporting young people. Within the COFOG framework, this expenditure is typically assigned to “Function 10.4 - Family and Children”, which falls under “Division 10 - Social Protection”. This category includes interventions such as child protection services, family allowances and youth assistance programmes. In the EU, social protection expenditure has remained relatively stable over the past decade, standing at around 19-20 % of GDP. A large majority of this spending is allocated to the COFOG expenditure category “old age” (approximately 10-11 % of GDP), while only a much smaller share (between 1,7 % and 2 %) is devoted to the category “families and children”  ( 21 ) . Over the years, the ratio between spending on old age and that on families and children has consistently hovered around 10 to 1. This is clearly influenced by population ageing and, consequently, pensions, which shift the structure of the welfare system away from investment in family policies and support for newborns.
4.3.
Another interesting experience in evaluating public policies is the Youth Check  ( 22 ) , which serves as a tool for ensuring that policies’ impact on young people is systematically factored in. This instrument allows for the labelling of intervention measures targeted at young people (generational measures), those that are potentially youth-oriented, and those that are ‘anti-generational’  ( 23 ) . There are already some regional and local  ( 24 ) experiences that show how generational and potentially generational measures for young people have been implemented through budget laws, highlighting the practical applicability of this classification in their formulation. In 2023, Italy’s Emilia-Romagna region experimented with generational impact assessment as part of its Safe-ER project, applying it to the 2021-2027 regional programmes co-financed by the ESF+ and the European Regional Development Fund  ( 25 ) . This was the first attempt to use generational impact assessment systematically at the regional and EU level, helping to establish a model that can be exported to other contexts. At local level, the Municipality of Parma was the first to apply generational impact assessment to its 2023-2025 ‘single programming document’ (DUP), accurately identifying the generational and potentially generational measures present in its planning documents. The administration has initiated a process of mapping public measures, classifying them according to the categories established by COVIGE (the Committee for the Assessment of the Generational Impact of Public Policies)  ( 26 ) and preparing the first Annual Report on Generational Impact Assessment, which presented the first evidence from the monitoring of generational and potentially generational measures.
4.4.
In order to identify age-related inequalities in public policy, the UN Economic Commission for Europe (UNECE) developed a methodology. This approach involves comparing different policy outcomes between different age groups and calculating an ‘ageing gap’. This would allow policy-makers to identify disparities and evaluate the inclusiveness of policies  ( 27 ) .
4.5.
The minimum threshold approach has been intensively adopted by the RRF, with the aim of promoting and supporting the dual green and digital transition, thanks to the introduction of targets and labelling. For the green transition, the Member States were required to allocate no less than 37 % of the resources received for this purpose, while for digitalisation, the minimum requirement was 20 %  ( 28 ) . To demonstrate compliance with these two targets, a labelling (or tagging or flagging) system was introduced, following the approach already tested in the ESF+, which requires national or regional investment plans to identify specific measures that contribute to achieving these targets.
5.    Specific comments
5.1.
In its opinion SOC/800  ( 29 ) , the EESC stressed that ‘[i]ntergenerational solidarity is crucial to overcoming age discrimination against old and young people and inequalities between generations in the context of the current demographic development. It is essential to design social policies and services that take a life-cycle approach and that are fair, accessible and available for all age groups. Younger and older people often experience discrimination simply because of their age’.
5.2.
In the same opinion, the EESC calls for intergenerational solidarity to be established as one of the objectives under the European Social Fund in the 2028-2034 MFF and its implementing regulations.
5.3.
Following these principles, and in order to facilitate public policies that ensure a balanced approach between different generations and take into account intergenerational fairness in the medium and long term, this own-initiative opinion aims to promote the introduction of ‘intergenerational budgeting’ by encouraging an approach that would foster better awareness of how resources are allocated by EU, national and local financial programming to the different generations. This should be done fully respecting Member States’ competences and budgetary autonomy. Such an approach should also promote youth co-participation, especially for the detection of potentially generational measures, using current tools already tested in some Member States, such as the Youth Test or the Youth Check.
5.4.
This intergenerational budgeting approach would enable policy-makers and the community to better understand who are the target beneficiaries of the resources allocated by public budgets and, through mitigation measures, would thus enable possible imbalances towards one generation to be corrected and make it possible to ensure that public resources are spent in the most efficient and balanced way possible. In this way, it can contribute to ensuring a real improvement in the allocation and targeting of investments in all areas from an intergenerational perspective, especially in the social, employment, training and health fields.
5.5.
Specifically, the EESC proposes that a mechanism similar to that applied in the case of the National Recovery and Resilience Plans and ESF+ be applied to EU cohesion policies to ensure adequate future resources for both younger generations (young people and children) and older generations (those over 65) by precisely identifying expenditure items and measures that should help achieve intergenerational equity.
Brussels, 18 September 2025.

1.    Conclusions and recommendations
1.1.
The EU hosts diverse cleantech ecosystems, from well-established industries such as wind power to emerging sectors like electrolysers, battery production, carbon capture, and water-efficient technologies. However, while the EU has strong expertise in research and development (R&D), the transition from innovation to commercial deployment remains problematic, especially when compared to global competitors such as China and the US.
1.2.
The EU is a net importer of cleantech in many sectors and relies heavily on China for solar panels, batteries and raw materials, creating a strategic risk. US and Chinese policies challenge Europe’s ability to increase investments and strengthen its cleantech industry, including in sectors where it is leading.
1.3.
The fragmented policies and funding mechanisms included in the European Green Deal only partially address the EU’s cleantech manufacturing ambitions. Uncoordinated EU and national policies and funding hamper efficiency, current State aid measures disproportionately benefit wealthier Member States and funding remains difficult to navigate by project developers. Global competitive distortions challenge the EU’s cleantech industry. If Europe adopts the right policies, it could turn energy and water-related challenges into opportunities for job creation, new skills and business growth.
1.4.
For all these reasons, the EESC calls on the Commission to:
—
Adopt a revised consolidated industrial strategic framework to support the production of cleantech for decarbonisation and water efficiency.
—
Recognise cleantech as a distinct industrial sector and support its development by designing technology roadmaps, de-risking innovation through pilots and partnerships, and enhancing funding – especially via Horizon Europe and the 10th Framework Programme (FP10).
—
Mainstream the EU’s cleantech goals across policy areas.
—
Simplify regulations and deploy infrastructure for market entry, address supply chain and public approval issues, and improve access to funding and intellectual property rights (IPR) protection for start-ups; foster collaboration across research centres, start-ups and industry to accelerate the commercialisation of new technologies, and promote innovation-friendly frameworks such as regulatory sandboxes under the Net-Zero Industry Act (NZIA).
—
Promote incentives for the circular economy, including for second-life use, local sourcing, and quotas or labels for recycled content.
—
Complement each technology roadmap with a human and social dimension roadmap to support the skills’ transition for all workers. Such roadmaps should integrate data provided by the Clean Energy Technology Observatory and European Skills Intelligence Observatory.
—
Where necessary, invest in up- and re-skilling policies that develop learning content in cleantech sectors, including a water dimension, while monitoring the effectiveness and impact of programmes that have already been launched (e.g. European Solar Academy, European Battery Academy).
—
Strengthen cleantech skills through an EU-wide assessment of labour shortages for the clean-energy and water-technology sector while ensuring high job quality and inclusive access for women and other disadvantaged groups. The Commission should establish a specific cleantech stream within the European Skills Intelligence Observatory under the Union of Skills to ensure rapid availability of those skills.
—
Develop tools such as an EU skills passport, harmonised certification, and stronger links between education and industry to ease transitions into net-zero jobs.
—
Boost EU cleantech manufacturing through a European Competitiveness Fund, repurposed Innovation Fund, and frontloaded EIB investments, while ensuring cohesion and small and medium-sized enterprises’ (SMEs) access.
—
Coordinate and streamline funding, reform State aid frameworks, and strengthen administrative capacities to improve fund absorption and market fairness.
—
Invest in regional cleantech clusters, electricity grids and capital market integration, while accelerating permitting.
—
Strengthen cleantech demand by implementing NZIA with mandatory non-price procurement criteria, green and water-efficient product quotas, clean water technologies and sustainability standards that account for embodied carbon.
—
Integrate decarbonisation and water efficiency into trade agreements, and build strategic partnerships to strengthen cleantech supply chains.
—
Constantly monitor the evolution of the EU’s cleantech sector and report on the outcomes of policy implementation.
2.    Background on the state of cleantech manufacturing in Europe
2.1.
Europe has seen a significant increase in cleantech investment since 2021, driven especially by battery cell manufacturing. However, in other sectors such as solar photovoltaic (PV), European companies heavily rely on imports, especially from China  ( 1 ) . While investments are spread across the EU, most projects are concentrated in a handful of countries.
2.2.
Macroeconomic conditions, including high interest rates, led to a slowdown in equity investments in cleantech in the EU in 2024, by 24 % year-on-year (from EUR 11.6 billion in 2023 to EUR 8.8 billion in 2024). The equity contraction was offset by debt investment worth EUR 23.4 billion in 2024, a significant improvement from EUR 7.9 billion in 2023  ( 2 ) .
2.3.
While the EU maintains a strong industrial footprint in cleantech, the EU cleantech landscape varies by sector. The solar PV industry faces restructuring due to global competition, while wind energy is growing slowly and is geographically uneven, putting competitiveness at risk. Battery production is expanding with gigafactories, but electric vehicle (EV) demand depends on financial incentives provided by governments. Heat pump production is rising despite macroeconomic hurdles. Electrolyser capacity is set to grow, yet investment and demand uncertainty persist. Carbon capture and storage is developing, and biogas is growing with policy support. The EU leads in geothermal and solar thermal ocean and maritime cleantech  ( 3 ) .
2.4.
Coordinated EU industrial policy can reduce the inefficiency of having 27 competing approaches to reindustrialisation. A robust EU industrial policy governance framework should go beyond what the European Commission has proposed and, where necessary, sectoral industrial strategies and common EU support programmes should be considered. The EU needs to move from a largely reactionary approach to a future-oriented industrial strategy.
2.5.
As the promoter of the EU Blue Deal flagship initiative, the EESC emphasises that clean technologies should be both energy- and water efficient, while horizontal measures, such as better data collection, expanding infrastructure, energy savings, digitalisation, and improving access to affordable energy and water are essential for boosting the competitiveness of EU cleantech manufacturing.
3.    Boosting the cleantech innovation ecosystem
3.1.
According to the International Energy Agency, only half of the technologies needed to achieve full decarbonisation are market-ready. The next generation of cleantech needs to be developed and deployed.
3.2.
More than one-fifth of clean technologies worldwide are developed in the EU. However, for many early-stage technologies, the EU is squandering resources because its innovation potential is not translating into manufacturing capabilities.
3.3.
In 2023, China, the EU and the US accounted for 85 % of public R&D spending, with USD 17.5 billion, USD 13.5 billion, and USD 11 billion invested respectively  ( 4 ) . Public investment in clean energy research and innovation (R&I) has been increasing in the EU, but private investment remains insufficient.
3.4.
The EESC calls on the Commission to:
3.4.1.
Design technology roadmaps for emerging technologies to support the upgrading of their Technology Readiness Level (TRL), outlining their role in achieving the 2040 and 2050 climate targets.
3.4.2.
Further strengthen European funding for cleantech R&I; protect and expand Horizon Europe funding, safeguarding it during the negotiations on the multiannual financial framework (MFF).
3.4.3.
Make cleantech a priority in the upcoming FP10 programme for 2028-34.
3.4.4.
De-risk technologies by supporting demonstration projects, pilot projects and the creation of public-private partnerships (including joint EU undertakings).
3.4.5.
Enforce the protection of IPRs and make funding mechanisms (such as the Innovation Fund) more accessible for start-ups.
4.    Access to critical raw materials and circularity
4.1.
Adopting circular economy principles can foster new economic opportunities and reduce reliance on critical materials. Establishing recyclability and resource efficiency standards would create strong incentives for industries to decrease dependence on primary raw materials.
4.2.
The EESC recommends the following:
4.2.1.
The upcoming Circular Economy Act should drive recycling investments and promote circular material use through digital technologies and business models.
4.2.2.
Member States should enhance their domestic mining and refining capacities for key minerals and midstream processing capabilities, while maintaining high environmental and social standards.
4.2.3.
Incentives should be provided for local sourcing of Circular Resources and Waste, with mandatory quotas or voluntary labels for recycled materials.
5.    Workforce deployment and skills
5.1.
Cleantech sectors have some of the highest (re)skilling needs. Deeper analysis of the social impact of deploying cleantech will be needed to anticipate and manage structural challenges.
5.2.
Jobs in clean technologies are growing faster than in the rest of the economy  ( 5 ) . An ambitious Clean Industrial Deal (CID) that supports EU located net-zero manufacturing can generate an additional 1.6 million jobs by 2035, rising to 2.1 million by 2040  ( 6 ) , and potentially more if the water dimension is taken into account.
5.3.
In this respect, the EESC recommends:
5.3.1.
Investing in strengthening cleantech skills, promoting targeted training, and conducting an EU-wide assessment of skills shortages in net-zero technology sectors, designing targeted learning programmes, and creating NZIA academies where needed.
5.3.2.
Constantly monitoring the cleantech workforce gap through the recently announced European Skills Intelligence Observatory. Cleantech should be given a key priority role in the observatory to deliver early warning alerts regarding skills shortages and ensure rapid availability of those skills on the labour market.
5.3.3.
Prioritising job attractiveness by maintaining high labour standards, aiming for secure, well-paid and socially respected jobs. The Quality Jobs Roadmap proposed in the CID should guide project assessment in the NZIA and the Critical Raw Materials Act (CRMA).
5.3.4.
Prioritising reskilling for disadvantaged groups such as older workers and those in precarious employment. Classifying net-zero jobs as shortage occupations can ensure financial stability during training until workers enter the labour market  ( 7 ) ; increase the workforce participation of women in Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics.
5.3.5.
Developing an EU skills passport and harmonisation of EU certification schemes.
5.3.6.
Establishing intermediate institutions that aim to bridge the gap between education and work, including partnerships between cleantech sectors and technical universities to strengthen workforce development  ( 8 ) .
5.3.7.
Aiming for a fair distribution of jobs among regions with declining industries or in need of restructuring  ( 9 ) , by making use of existing funding streams (e.g. Just Transition Fund).
6.    Unlocking investments
6.1.
As fiscal room is limited, existing funding programmes should be focused on those stages of the cleantech value chains where the EU can develop comparative advantages. The EU should seek to raise additional common European funding for financing its industrial ambitions.
6.2.
The end of NextGenerationEU in 2027 will lead to EUR 35 billion of net-zero investment being discontinued, creating a financing gap  ( 10 ) that could be partly offset through the upcoming Industrial Decarbonisation Fund, a future EU Blue Deal Transition Fund or the envisaged European Competitiveness Fund (next MFF).
6.3.
The current State aid framework has driven investments but also caused market distortions and regional disparities persist. From 2022 to 2023, a few leading regions increased investments by USD 15-17 billion, while Southern, Central and Eastern Europe saw only a USD 3 billion rise  ( 11 ) .
6.4.
To make financial support (both public and private) even more effective, the EESC supports the following proposals:
6.4.1.
Creating a European Competitiveness Fund in the new MFF, potentially supported by new EU joint borrowing via a European safe asset (2026). The fund should support growth equity and target clean technology value chains, aiming to foster European cohesion and prevent a two-speed Europe.
6.4.2.
The Innovation Fund should be transformed into a deployment fund and earmark a share for cleantech manufacturing. More attention should be paid to improving access to such instruments for SMEs.
6.4.3.
Notwithstanding social objectives, mandating Member States to invest at least 25 % of their Emissions Trading System (ETS) revenues in cleantech manufacturing, including by using the Auction-as-a-Service  ( 12 ) function of the Innovation Fund. Spending plans should be included in National Energy and Climate Plans (NECPs)  ( 13 ) .
6.4.4.
Streamlining and coordinating all funding devoted to the manufacturing of cleantech, for example by using centralised portals such as the Strategic Technologies for Europe Platform; coordinating and harmonising national support schemes, setting up European one-stop shops and uniform application procedures.
6.4.5.
Frontloading cleantech investments made possible through ETS revenues, including through European Investment Bank (EIB) borrowing.
6.4.6.
Facilitating cleantech innovation by deepening capital markets and making it easier for start-ups and scale-ups to access risk capital, especially through a Capital Markets Union.
6.4.7.
Stepping up the role of the EIB (and national promotional banks) in fostering private investments through the expansion of (counter) guarantees to include cleantech sectors.
6.4.8.
Creating regional cleantech clusters, especially in transitioning areas, by using smart specialisation and existing funds, and by promoting active collaboration between all stakeholders, linking public resources to social and environmental criteria.
6.4.9.
Simplifying State aid procedures under the forthcoming Clean Industrial State Aid Framework, building on insights from the Temporary Crisis and Transition Framework and the General Block Exemption Regulation, while aiming to ensure regional fairness and avoid distortions to the single market.
6.4.10.
Reforming IPCEIs and providing financial and administrative support to help low-income regions join EU value chains more easily, including by strengthening administrative capacity in countries struggling to absorb funds.
6.4.11.
Accelerating planning and permitting procedures for new cleantech projects.
6.4.12.
Investing massively in modernising and connecting European electricity grids as deployment of cleantech is currently being hampered by the slow progress of electrification.
7.    Developing markets and lead market creation
7.1.
Many clean technologies are still emerging and require stronger market uptake. This can be supported by incentivising adoption by the private sector and by embedding local content and resilience criteria into both public and private procurement processes.
7.2.
Auctions under NZIA should include criteria for the water consumption and for responsible business conduct, cybersecurity and execution capabilities, with sustainability and resilience factors accounting for 15-30 %.
7.3.
To further strengthen European lead markets, the EESC calls for the following:
7.3.1.
The NZIA should be implemented through public procurement and renewable energy auctions that include mandatory non-price criteria (including social conditionalities). Sustainability standards must be strengthened to reflect the carbon and water footprint of materials used in net-zero technologies, going well beyond current benchmarks  ( 14 ) .
7.3.2.
Member States should enhance regulations to drive demand for renewable products by integrating explicit sustainability and resilience criteria.
7.3.3.
A net-zero ‘EU-value-chain bonus’ and quotas for green, water-efficient products in key sectors like steel and batteries could help restore Europe’s cleantech leadership. To accelerate industrial decarbonisation, the Industrial Accelerator Decarbonisation Act could set similar quotas, such as clean steel use in cars and wind turbines.
7.3.4.
Introducing common EU product passports (e.g. battery passports), quality labels or mandatory carbon and water footprint declarations for products would increase transparency, helping consumers and businesses make informed decisions (including export markets).
7.3.5.
The cost premium of clean technology solutions should be reduced through mechanisms such as contracts for difference for energy or fixed premium subsidies linked to the environmental performance of products.
8.    Levelling the international playing field and establishing cooperation
8.1.
Europe’s cleantech sector faces mounting pressure from global subsidies, looser environmental standards and unfair competition, leading to increased dependence on third countries. A growing trade deficit with China, driven by its dominance in rare earths, State-sponsored industrial strategies and low-price exports, highlights Europe’s competitiveness challenges. The EU lags behind in venture capital, attracting only 5 % compared to the US’ 52 %, limiting its ability to scale up innovations. The EU must boost domestic production, diversify resources and coordinate international trade and industrial policies to ensure fair competition and resilient supply chains.
8.2.
The EESC recommends that:
8.2.1.
Trade agreements dedicate specific chapters to decarbonisation, water efficiency and cleantech. These chapters should promote the deployment of cleantech, secure supply chains and support market access.
8.2.2.
The EU must build strategic industrial partnerships with like-minded countries to strengthen supply chain resilience, as full value chain control as pursued by China and the US is unlikely. Clean Trade and Investment Partnerships can enhance cooperation, but the EU must clarify its value proposition to partners.
8.2.3.
The EU should strengthen trade defence, modernise energy infrastructure through the Global Gateway, and attract investment while promoting technology transfer. It should balance free trade benefits with sustainability, ensuring responsible mineral sourcing and supply chain due diligence.
8.2.4.
Options for promoting cleantech exports through World Trade Organization-compliant instruments should be explored.

title: Opinion of the European Economic and Social Committee – A challenge for the single market: a European defence policy well balanced with the needs of citizens (own-initiative opinion)
text:

EN

Opinion of the European Economic and Social Committee
A challenge for the single market: a European defence policy well balanced with the needs of citizens
(own-initiative opinion)
(C/2026/4)
Rapporteur :
Angelo PAGLIARA
Advisor
Simone D'ALESSANDRO (to the rapporteur)
Plenary Assembly decision

Legal basis

Section responsible

Outcome of vote
(for/against/abstentions)

1.    Conclusions and recommendations
1.1.
The EESC reiterates that the strengthening of the EU’s defensive capacities must be implemented in accordance with its fundamental values, placing economic, social and territorial cohesion at its core, as provided for in Article 3 TEU. An effective defence policy can only exist if it is embedded in a European project geared towards the well-being of the public.
1.2.
The EESC believes that, from a security perspective, the EU should adopt a common defence policy as part of a shared foreign and security policy, and build a strong European defence pillar, going beyond national models and the resulting fragmented expenditure. The legislative and financial measures that are needed to achieve this should be rolled out as a matter of urgency and within a common framework, also in consideration of the risks that the European countries bordering Russia and Belarus are facing.
1.3.
The EESC calls for an integrated approach to European security, covering not just military needs but also the social, industrial, environmental and health aspects. The EU’s resilience relies on strong public systems and the trust of the public. The well-being of European citizens in today’s geopolitical context cannot be ensured without an adequate level of defence capabilities and societal preparedness. True resilience is built on the capacity to respond to external aggression and on the strength of public systems to protect citizens in all aspects of life.
1.4.
The EESC stresses the urgent need to strengthen the Single Market by overcoming the fragmentation of the defence market by promoting a common European industrial policy that enhances industrial competitiveness while respecting the principles of transparency, efficiency and sustainability. It also calls for specific common funding instruments to be adopted.
1.5.
The EESC recommends that defence investment be geared towards strengthening the European defence technological and industrial base (EDTIB), actively involving the social partners and small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) as key players in local production chains. It is essential to promote skilled employment and prevent harmful dumping or offshoring practices, so as to ensure that the benefits are felt widely across Europe’s production system.
1.6.
The EESC considers it essential to ensure proper coordination between European funding instruments and the EU fiscal framework, by laying down rules that allow strategic investments, including those in the defence sector, to be excluded from deficit calculations, by means of fiscal escape clauses consistent with the EU’s objectives.
1.7.
The EESC calls on the Commission and the Member States to ensure full transparency on the origin, destination and governance of defence funds, so that the increase in spending does not come at the expense of other key EU objectives, public services or health.
1.8.
The EESC would like to see the establishment of an inter-institutional observatory for integrated security (involving the EESC, the CoR, the Commission and the Parliament) to monitor the impact of European defence policies at local level and systematically measure how they are perceived and the extent to which they are trusted by the public.
2.    General comments
2.1.
Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 and the geopolitical events of recent months have prompted the European institutions to place the issue of European defence at the top of the political agenda. The war highlighted Europe’s dependence on U.S. support to ensure its defence while exposing gaps in its capacities. At the same time, worrying uncertainty in Transatlantic relations highlighted how the EU is facing a sudden and urgent need to find swift and united responses to a multitude of challenges and potential threats in the military, trade, technology and procurement spheres. In this context, particular attention should be devoted to EU Member States bordering Russia and Belarus, as they are the most directly exposed to immediate crises and hybrid threats.
2.2.
The EU has a history of failed defence integration attempts since the 1954 European Defence Community (EDC). This opinion aims to feed into the European debate. It starts with the premise that the geopolitical context requires decisive action to build a common defence system. The challenge is how to invest in common defence, completing the single market, without compromising social cohesion and investment in the well-being of Europeans and while ensuring compliance with the Treaties.
2.3.
Article 3 of the Treaty on European Union (TEU) points out that the Union’s aim is to promote the well-being of its peoples, economic and social cohesion, and balanced and harmonious development of the Member States. From this perspective, European defence policy is expected to integrate these aspects and support the attainment of these objectives, so as to ensure a peaceful and secure life for EU citizens.
2.4.
In the context of this opinion, the EESC builds on many other documents it has already adopted – as well as documents that are currently being drawn up – in the field of defence and security, and in particular on a number of opinions that deal with the subject in depth and in a structured way  ( 1 ) . These opinions set out a comprehensive and coherent picture of the role that defence can play in building European sovereignty that is in line with the values of peace, democracy and social justice.
2.5.
The Union’s ability to enhance its common defence and address geopolitical and industrial challenges is closely linked to action to enhance European integration. The EESC calls on the Commission and the Council to explore all mechanisms set out in the Treaties in order to lose no time in activating a process of institutional reform and move forward with the completion of the integration process.
2.6.
The political debates and divisions within the EU related to the Commission’s recent defence proposals show that the balance between defence spending and social investment is crucial. A Union that is stronger in military terms must also be fairer, more cohesive and more resilient for its people.
3.    Specific comments
3.1.
The Draghi report  ( 2 ) shows that between 2022 and 2023, 78 % of European military spending went to non-EU suppliers and 63 % of that went to the US. This dependence limits the EU’s strategic autonomy, increasing geopolitical risk and exposing European security to the industrial and policy choices of third-party actors. In addition, the fragmentation of procurement among Member States is an obstacle to the creation of a single market for defence, leaving European industry vulnerable to the major global powers and preventing the establishment of the common standards needed for interoperability and industrial efficiency.
3.2.
The lack of coordination in defence procurement distorts the internal market, favours industries outside Europe and limits the growth of production and research inside Europe. According to the Italian Public Accounts Observatory (Osservatorio sui conti pubblici italiani), in 2024 the EU’s total military expenditure was significantly higher than that of Russia in purchasing-power parity (PPP) terms  ( 3 ) . However, the lack of a shared strategy among Member States reduces its overall effectiveness. The fragmentation of production and procurement prevents resources from being used strategically, making the European defence sector less competitive than the more centralised Russian sector. In this regard, the lack of standardisation when it comes to technical requirements and weapon systems is a real obstacle to interoperability, logistical efficiency and cost reduction (in this context, it is equally important to ensure alignment with NATO standards). To reduce this dependency and strengthen the EU’s strategic autonomy, it is necessary first and foremost to accelerate the completion of the single market for defence by harmonising regulations, investing in research and development, improving interoperability between national systems and establishing a stable joint procurement mechanism that allows Member States to prioritise European suppliers, avoiding the scattering of resources.
3.3.
The EU needs a robust defence framework capable of dealing not only with immediate crises but also with long-term challenges. This requires a strong industrial base capable of supporting technological development, guaranteeing strategic autonomy and ensuring that investments have a positive impact on economic growth and employment. Without a clear industrial policy, defence plans may be ineffective. The EESC stresses the need to step up investment in industrial policies, including by establishing a European sovereign fund able to finance common strategic projects.
3.4.
A European defence industry strategy should also involve the EESC and the Committee of the Regions in a structured way, fostering resilient local production chains. The employment potential of industrial restructuring can only translate into stable, quality jobs if relocations and social dumping practices are avoided, ensuring fair and inclusive conditions for all European economic stakeholders.
3.5.
The EESC believes that the legislative and financial measures needed to strengthen European defence should be adopted within an EU framework. A common financing system, based on the coordination of expenditure and the optimisation of resources, would enhance the internal market, avoid waste and maximise the effectiveness of investments, while reducing dependence on non-European suppliers. The latest macroeconomic forecasts suggest that significant structural effects on the economy cannot be generated from defence spending on its own. For this reason, the impact of defence spending must be considered within a broader strategy that includes coordinated public investment in the social and industrial spheres  ( 4 ) .
3.6.
In a decade, military spending in Europe has increased by an average of 50 %, from EUR 145 billion in 2014 to EUR 215 billion in 2023  ( 5 ) . The EESC emphasises that strengthening the EU’s defence capabilities is also an opportunity to revitalise Europe’s industrial and technological base. Some analyses, including the Draghi Report and the European Commission’s Spring 2025 Economic Forecast, suggest that coordinated increases in defence spending could contribute to GDP growth, job creation and innovation. For example, a simulation using the QUEST model estimates that a gradual increase in defence expenditure by Member States up to 1,5 % of GDP by 2028 could raise EU GDP by about 0,5 % by the end of that period, with a parallel increase of approximately 2 percentage points in the debt-to-GDP ratio. However, the effectiveness of such spending is not automatic: its impact depends heavily on the degree of industrial coordination and the development of an integrated internal defence market. In the absence of a shared strategy, the economic multiplier of defence spending risks remaining low, particularly due to the high share of extra- EU imports, as shown by recent input-output analyses. Common standards, interoperability and joint procurement mechanisms are essential to ensure that defence investments generate lasting benefits and contribute meaningfully to the EU’s strategic autonomy.
3.7.
Investment in the defence sector must be embedded within a strategy aimed at strengthening the EU’s production chains, spurring on innovation and attracting skilled workers. Greater industrial coordination at European level – by means of common standards, interoperability and joint procurement – has the potential to increase the economic multiplier effect of defence spending. Without this coordination, the risk is that the multiplier effect will remain limited due to the high proportion of imports from outside the EU, as demonstrated in recent studies based on input-output analyses  ( 6 ) . Developing an integrated internal market for defence must therefore be a priority in order to support the EU’s strategic autonomy.
3.8.
Data from the latest 2024 Living Conditions Report show an overall deterioration: 19,1 % of European households struggle to make ends meet (compared to 16,8 % in 2020); the share of people at risk of poverty or social exclusion has risen to 16,5 % (up from 14,3 % in 2019); income inequality has increased from 28,7 % to 29,6 %; severe material and social deprivation has continued to increase, rising from 6,7 % to 6,8 %; and the share of households unable to meet unexpected expenses stands at 33,5 % (up from 30,2 % in 2020). Life expectancy fell from 81.3 years in 2019 to 80.1 in 2023  ( 7 ) . This deterioration is also confirmed by the Parliament’s 2024 Eurobarometer survey, which found that Europeans’ main concerns are rising prices and the cost of living (42 %) and the economic situation (41 %). These data point to a deterioration in social conditions that, if not addressed, could well undermine the very foundations of European security.
3.9.
The bolstering of the European health system should be viewed as a pillar of the European defence system. The latest available reports point to persistent structural weaknesses in national health systems: staff shortages, insufficient infrastructure and unequal access to services  ( 8 ) . The EESC believes that, in the present geopolitical context, the need to ramp up investment in health is incompatible with the current Stability and Growth Pact, which is an obstacle to the pursuit of the EU’s goals of security and social resilience.
3.10.
In times of crisis, support for the institutions from the people of Europe and civil society is crucial. The EESC calls on the Commission to explore the possibility of establishing an inter-institutional observatory comprising the EESC, the CoR, the Commission and the Parliament, with the specific task of monitoring how European decisions are perceived in the Member States and promoting a concept of common European defence that factors in the social, economic and health aspects. Transparency, democratic accountability and civic engagement are essential conditions for building public trust in the European institutions. In the absence of trust, even the most advanced security policies risk losing their effectiveness and legitimacy. The observatory should help to monitor not just the local impact of European defence choices, but also public trust in them and how they are perceived by society.
3.11.
The EESC stresses that European security is based on an integrated approach, where defence capabilities are combined with the strength of the EU’s soft power: cooperation, diplomacy, and the promotion of development and stability. Preserving and strengthening this balance is essential for the EU to play a credible and autonomous role on the global stage.
Brussels, 18 September 2025.
